speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief statement with respect to Canadian representation on the united nations atomic energy commission.
It will be recalled that on January 25 of the present year the general assembly of the united nations, meeting in London, provided for the establishment of a commission to deal
Postal Service

with the urgent and important problems raised by the discovery of atomic energy and other related matters.
It was also provided in the resolution adopted by the assembly that the commission should be composed of one representative from each of those states represented on the security council, and Canada when this country was not a member of the security council. Each national representative on the commission was to have such assistance as might be desired.
The secretary general of the united nations has now asked the government of Canada to appoint a representative to this important commission and an order in council has accordingly been passed appointing General the Honourable Andrew G. L. McNaughton, C.B., C.M.G., D.S.O., as Canadian representative.
General McNaughton will be assisted by an advisory panel consisting of appropriate officials of the Departments of Reconstruction and Supply, External Affairs, and National Defence, and including the president of the national research council. The membership of the panel will be flexible according to the nature of the questions coming before it for consideration, and provision has been made for adding persons with special knowledge to this group of advisers as and when it may be deemed desirable.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief statement regarding recent developments in price ceiling policy.
During the past few days, as hon. members no doubt will have noticed, the wartime prices and trade board has authorized a number of important price adjustments. Ceiling prices for iron and steel and for various consumer articles made from iron and steel have been increased. Producers of lumber will be permitted to charge higher prices, although wholesalers' and retailers' ceilings. remain unchanged. Butter and pork prices have been raised. Price increases have been permitted for various pulp and paper products other than newsprint. In the course of the next three or four months small increases will take place in the retail prices of clothing and furnishings consequent upon the government's decision to eliminate subsidies on imports of raw cotton and wool.
Taken in conjunction with the decision made at the beginning of February to suspend price ceilings on a list of some 300 items and with the relaxation of rigid price controls on many imported goods, these recent steps may be regarded by some as implying that price control is breaking down, or at least that the basic policy of the government has been changed.
I am therefore taking this opportunity of making it plain that such is not the case. These adjustments are part and parcel of a -arefully planned programme which has been developing gradually since V-E day, and which, in its broad outlines, has been

Price Control
explained to the house and to the public on several occasions during the past twelve months. These measures do not mean that the government's anti-inflation policy as administered by the prices board is beginning to falter. They do not mean that we contemplate an early lifting of our price control system, nor must they be taken to imply that any serious increase in the cost of living is impending. On the contrary, they indicate that the government is prepared to maintain control over the movement of prices during this difficult and highly dangerous transition period.
I need hardly say that the danger of inflation is still very great. Many commodities are still in short supply, e.g., food, textiles and building materials-all highly essential. Purchasing power and consumer demands exceed their war-time levels. In this situation it would be unthinkable to allow prices to find their own level. But that does not mean, of course, that the administration of price control should not change. The system which served Canada so well in war must now be adapted, and is being adapted, to meet the special circumstances of the transition period.
Our system of price control has always permitted price adjustments in cases of genuine necessity. The special significance of the adjustments recently announced arises from the fact that they cover a wider area of Canadian industry than has so far been affected. I believe, however, that this will be recognized as the sensible approach to the problem. It would be folly to pretend that the government could continue to administer the same more or less inflexible system of price ceilings that was appropriate to the uncertain days of 1942 and i943. Here and there the line has to bend if it is not to break.
The declared aim of the government's price policy for the transition period is to give a reasonable degree of stability to living costs while creating conditions favorable to a high level of employment and production. In practice this means that where the wartime prices and trade board is satisfied that production is capable of expanding on the basis of basic period selling prices, then basic period prices will continue as the legal maxima. On the other hand, where it can be demonstrated to the satisfaction of the prices board that present ceiling prices are prejudicially affecting production and employment, adjustments are made. But except for commodities in quite ample supply, or relatively unimportant, price ceilings are. not suspended.
As the house will realize, it is easy to state general principles such as these but more
difficult to put them into practice. The prices board is literally in a continuous fight to prevent- price increases from being extended any further than is absolutely necessary. The increases in prices, to which I referred earlier, provide examples of the policy in practice. In the case of iron and steel, the support of the price structure formerly given by war production has disappeared. Consequently, wartime increases in .costs must now be reflected in selling prices of the basic iron and steel products. The wartime accumulation of cost increases, particularly wage increases, is also the basic factor behind the increase in the producer's price of soft-wood lumber, and in pulp and paper prices.
Another factor behind certain recent price increases stems from the decision which the government reached some time ago to reduce or eliminate subsidy payments. While subsidies played a vital part in checking the forces of inflation during the war, they are not desirable as a permanent feature of the price structure, and should be removed as expeditiously as possible. Certain subsidies were paid to offset temporary wartime cost increases and are more or less self-liquidating. The subsidies formerly paid on imports of petroleum are a good example of what I mean. On the other hand, it looks as if the wartime increase in the cost of imported cotton and wool, for example, is more or less permanent. In view of this, the board has largely withdrawn from the payment of subsidies on wool imports in recent months, and has reduced the amount of subsidy paid on cotton imports. At the same time, the prices board has authorized certain price increases that will be necessary to compensate for the higher price of wool and cotton as the various products move from the mills and converters, through to the garment manufacturers and down to the final consumer. The price increases authorized have been carefully worked out in relation to seasonal production, and in relation to inventories and other such factors, and the board is confident that the increase of consumer prices will be kept to the bare minimum necessary to offset subsidies. In other words, basic period or 1941 price ceilings in this particular industry, as in other industries where adjustments are necessary, will cease to be the rule, but the system of legal maximum price ceilings remains intact.
The recent increases in the prices of butter and pork products require very little explanation. In the case of butter, an additional incentive is needed if even a restricted consumer ration is to be met. In the case of bacon, the United Kingdom, realizing that hog numbers were declining seriously, agreed
International Trade

to raise contract prices immediately, and the domestic price was simply adjusted to the new level.
I am confident that the policy we have been following is capable of meeting the realities of this period of adjustment. It will undoubtedly mean a modest increase in the cost of living. But it will enable us to preserve the economic advantages we have gained from nearly five years of self-discipline on the economic front, and will protect consumers and producers alike from the economic and social dislocation which would surely develop if present inflationary pressures were given free rein.
In conclusion I wish to reiterate that the government has no intention of putting into effect what some political and other groups are advocating, namely, the removal, wholly or substantially, of price control.
We believe that price control and the maintenance of ceilings have the support of the Canadian people and we do not intend at this stage of the fight to flout their opinion or destroy the results of nearly five years of determined effort to prevent inflation.
I would like to appeal to this house and to the Canadian people for continued support of measures which we are satisfied are necessary if economic stability is to be maintained, if the real value of our currency and our bonds is to be protected, and if the bankruptcy and unemployment resulting from a price boom followed by a price collapse are to be avoided.

I should like to address
a question to the Minister of Finance on his statement, regarding the price of butter. Did I understand the minister to say that this arises out of a withdrawal of the subsidy to the producers of butter fat?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: ORDER IN COUNCIL CREATING CANADIAN COMMERCIAL CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table order in council P.C. 1218 of March 29, 1916, which authorizes the creation of the Canadian Commercial Corporation. I would like to make a brief statement to explain some of the main functions of this corporation.
In view of the many transactions which require immediate attention, it has been necessary to bring the corporation into being by means of order in council. Legislation

will be presented at this session to enable the corporation to operate on a continuing basis for a period.
For some time it has been clear that there are many transactions in international trade which cannot be handled entirely by private enterprise and the work of the corporation is intended to supplement the activities of business organization rather than to interfere with them.
The Canadian Commercial Corporation will, firstly, take over the various functions of making purchases in this country for foreign governments and the united nations relief and rehabilitation administration that have hitherto been performed by the Canadian Export Board. The value of such purchases made to date by the Canadian Export Board exceeds $417,000,000.
Secondly, the Canadian Commercial Corporation will assist private enterprise in obtaining essential supplies from ex-enemy territories. Supplies from such territories cannot be obtained at present through ordinary commercial channels.
Thirdly, this corporation provides the machinery which could be used in the future to purchase commodities such as sugar, tea, oils and fats which are under international allocation or foreign government control and may continue to be so for some time to come.
It is impossible at the moment to enumerate in full detail all the functions that will be discharged by the corporation. The three main purposes that I have outlined are only an indication of the work to be performed. New tasks may devolve upon the corporation, as its work proceeds, in the light of its developing experience and the needs of Canadian business.
The creation of the Canadian Commercial Corporation enables the government to provide facilities to Canadian business that will match those being offered to British and American traders through the operations of the United Kingdom Commercial Corporation and the United States Commercial Corporation.
The executive officer who will be charged with the primary responsibility for directing the activities of the corporation will be its director and general manager, Mr. W. D. Low, who assumes these new duties after having been chairman of the Canadian Export Board, and prior to that, executive assistant to the deputy minister of the Department of Munitions and Supply, where he had supervision over the purchasing branches. He is on loan from the purchasing department in Montreal of the Canadian National Railways.

maintopic: $10,000.000. HOUSE OF COMMONS STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RESIGNATION OF MEMBER FOR PARKDALE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: $10,000.000. HOUSE OF COMMONS STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RESIGNATION OF MEMBER FOR PARKDALE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a word about the resignation of the hon. member for Parkdale, Mr. Bruce, which was announced to the house last night, and the reference made by Your Honour to the fact that you are issuing a writ to-day for a new election.
What I am about to say is said solely with the intention of bringing to the attention of hon. members of the house what I believe to be the spirit if not the letter of the parliamentary law with respect to a member of parliament relinquishing his seat in the House of Commons. Do not let it be assumed for one moment that I take any exception to the hon. member for Parkdale having resigned his seat, or that I am criticizing his action in so doing. Such is not the case. I believe there is a certain responsibility upon myself as the leader of the house to draw the attention of the house to what is quite evidently, according to the authorities, the spirit of the parliamentary law with respect to resignations of members of the House of Commons.
The House of Commons Act does not set forth any reason for a member's resignation. Section 6 says, "Any member of the House of Commons may resign his seat" either by giving notice in his place in the house or by addressing a written declaration of his intention to resign attested by two witnesses. Nevertheless it may I think be truly said that a member is elected to serve during the life of a parliament. Unless there are grave reasons compelling him to return to private life, or he receives some appointment underthe crown he is, I believe, in duty bound to keep the mandate he has received from his constituents. Sir Erskine May says in his thirteenth edition, at page 45:
It is ia settled principle of parliamentary law that a member after he is duly chosen, cannot relinquish his seat.
This restriction can be evaded in the United Kingdom by a member accepting an office under the crown, usually the Chiltern Hundreds, an office which is merely nominal though assuming the form of a place of profit. The evasion takes place only when there are grave or very special reasons for it. It would nor be acceptable if a member wished to resign when he becomes weary of political life or feels that parliamentary work interferes with his personal affairs.
Redlich, Procedure of the House of Commons, volume 2, at page 99, says:
It is well known that English parliamentary law recognizes no power on the part of a member to relinquish his seat.
Bourinot, fourth edition, at page 157, says:
It was formerly a principle of parliamentary law that a member after he is duly chosen cannot relinquish his seat.
There can be no doubt that the hon. member for Parkdale had the right to resign without giving any reason for taking that step, but he has taken a course which may establish a dangerous precedent. The House of Commons Act, in prescribing the way in which a member may resign, cannot have intended to make resignation easy, and applicable on the slightest provocation. The cause of it, it would appear, should be prompted by public rather than personal interest.

Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved the second reading of bill No. 6, to amend the Department of External Affairs Act.
He said: The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, as I explained at the time of its introduction, is to repeal section (3) of the Department of External Affairs Act, which was enacted in 1912 by the administration of Sir Robert Borden, and which provides that-
The member of the King's Privy Council for Canada holding the recognized position of First Minister shall be the 'Secretary of State for External Affairs . . .
As it stands the section constitutes a statutory requirement that the Secretary of State for External Affairs can be no one . but the Prime Minister. The present bill would remove this limitation and make it possible for some other person to occupy the position. The result of the present bill will be to place the "Department of External Affairs in precisely the same position as the other departments of government in respect of which there is no requirement that any particular person must occupy the position of minister. That is all there is to the present bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire first of all to say to the Prime Minister that some years ago in the House of Commons a very eminent counsel who sat in this chamber for a good many years was asked to what he attributed his great success in the courts of Canada. His answer was that it was probably attributable to the fact that when he had the judge supporting his case in court he never tried to argue with the judge. There does seem to be an analogy to that in the matter now before us, because to-day we have the government with us in respect to a change in the legislation dealing with external affairs.
While perhaps we should not deny to the Prime Minister the immediate fatherhood of this measure may I say that its ancestry, as I think the right hon. gentleman will agree, goes much beyond the party now in power. Almost continuously and consistently since 1943 this official opposition has made an appeal, and in many instances an urgent appeal, for legislation such as that now introduced. The appeal was made in 1943, again in 1944 and in 1945, and again at the beginning of this session. I think hon. members will recall, and by reference will see, that there is now on the order paper a resolution proposed by myself

I hope my hon. friend will not be too technical. If he is, I may decide to argue the point. However, I have not yet started to read the resolution, nor have I done more than suggest that I was going to give some salient points of it. Perhaps my hon. friend did not hear what I said. In the resolution I indicated that the Department of External Affairs had grown in size and importance to the point where a full-time minister was both vital and essential in the national interest.
In addition it will be recognized by every hon. member in this house that Canada's responsibility abroad has increased to the point where external affairs has become one of the major businesses of government and one of the principal concerns of parliament.
I shall not repeat what I said in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne when I dealt with this point, other than to say that it is a matter of vital necessity that a minister who has had the advantage of a close liaison or connection, knitting-in or meshing, with the men under him in the Department of External Affairs, should represent Canada at international gatherings. As I pointed out in my address at that time, without any reflection upon those who had represented Canada in a leading capacity at various international gatherings I was afraid that as time went on we should witness an extraordinary situation-that of the Prime Minister, because of his numerous and onerous duties in the domestic field, finding it impossible to attend all the international gatherings and having to substitute some other minister of the crown who may not always be conversant with the many moves that are taking place in the international field. We should then find ourselves with a delegation led by someone who perhaps while at the conference would have to learn many of the lessons on external affairs. This was one of the reasons which prompted me to place on the order paper for consideration in due course the resolution to which I have referred.
I wish to say to the Prime Minister that so far as our party is concerned we are prepared to accept and give support to the second reading of a bill which will enable this government to appoint someone as fulltime minister of external affairs. Most hon. members will realize, particularly those who

have gone to international conferences, that there is scarcely any nation in the world which is not led either by the head of the state, the prime minister, or the minister of foreign affairs. Australia, which is not as large a country as Canada, has had for some considerable time its own foreign minister, who in the conclaves of the world has done an exceedingly effective job on behalf of his country. Such nations as Denmark, Czechoslovakia, Norway, Belgium, and the Netherlands, to say nothing of many smaller countries, are represented at international conferences by their prime ministers, the ministers of external affairs or foreign ministers. No nation of Canada's size and importance can go longer without a full-time minister of external affairs.
I have only this criticism to offer. I think the government mig^t properly have brought in this bill a year ago. After all, many pieces of legislation which contemplated the peacetime reconstruction era were brought in at the last session. We can no longer take the risk of going without this measure. We should have in harness at this very moment a minister of external affairs. The fact that on two occasions at least the Prime Minister has said that he will not, run in another general election is an additional reason why this matter should be taken care of.

Mr. M. J. COLD WELL (Rosetown-Biggar) Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the proposal now before the house. We are not recent converts to this point of view. My predecessor, the late Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, who was leader of this movement from its inception in 1933, used to offer the suggestion from time to time in the house that we needed a separate and full-time minister of external affairs.
We have always believed that Canada had grown to a stature, even during the years which intervened between the two wars, that entitled her to representation by a full-time minister. In saying this, let it be understood that I am not detracting in any way from the services rendered by the Prime Minister in that department. Let me make that perfectly clear.
I do believe however that the duties of the office of Prime Minister and those [DOT]of the Secretary of State for External Affairs are to-day so onerous that no one individual, no matter how capable, can prop, erly discharge them. In our opinion, therefore, the appointment of a full-time minister is long overdue. The very fact that we appointed last session and are reappointing this session a committee on external affairs makes it necessary that we have a minister who can devote his whole attention to the department and can sit with the committee. In the years I have been in the house-and before, because I read Hansard assiduously before I came-I have considered it tragic that so little attention has been given by Parliament to the affairs of this department.
I noted before the war that usually the *estimates of the Department of External Affairs came pretty well toward the end of the session. Occasionally by agreement among the parties in the house a day was set aside when an item might be discussed, but with the exception of a handful of people in parliament there were few who between the two wars really took the interest in external .affairs which that dpartment of government -warranted.

Whatever may have been Canada's position among the nations before the present war, I think we are all agreed that in every respect she has now attained the stature of full nationhood. We have the obligations that come with nationhood. We have in Ottawa the representatives of many governments of the world, in the persons of ambassadors and ministers, and we in turn are represented in many other countries. There was a time when perhaps a British ambassador or a British consul might represent Canada, but that is no longer true. While we have the closest association, and must maintain it, with the British commonwealth of nations, we must never forget that we are a nation in our own right. As we have discovered in these international conferences, the component parts of the British commonwealth of nations do not speak with a single voice. If that needed to be demonstrated it was evident at San Francisco, it was evident at London, and at the recent meeting of the security council it was demonstrated anew by the action of the representative of Australia.
I have felt for a long time, years indeed, that we should have a full time minister in charge of this department. Canada has been particularly fortunate, and the Prime Minister as minister of external affairs has been particularly fortunate, in the type of personnel that has been gathered together in the Department of External Affairs. Nothing impressed me more deeply than the capability and the breadth of vision of the advisers who accompanied us to San Francisco. My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who was present at the meetings of the united nations organization and the assembly in London, came back with exactly the same report, that Canada's external affairs officials and advisers compared favourably with those of any other country in the world. I am glad to have this opportunity of paying this tribute to them.
Our status as a nation makes us independent, yet we are associated with the British commonwealth of nations by many ties which I hope will be continued throughout the years. Canada is a nation in her own right. She speaks at interntional conferences as a nation independent of the United States, independent of Great Britain-speaks always as Canada. I believe the time has come when we should assume all the obligations of that position. We should have responsible to this house a minister of external affairs who will be prepared from time to time to meet the external affairs committee of this house in order that we as a parliament may understand more completely

External Affairs
the international obligations of Canada and be more fully aware of the policies that are being followed.
In a statement which he made to the house this afternoon the Prime Minister referred to the fact that while Canada is not to be a member of the security council, she is to become a member of the commission dealing with atomic power, because of the importance of Canada's contribution in regard to that great and in some respects terrifying, in other respects encouraging, discovery, with the implications of which the world now has to deal.
I am speaking not only for myself but for those associated with me in my party. As I have said, for many years we have put forward resolutions urging the members of parliament to provide for the appointment of a minister of external affairs, and we are glad to see that that is to be done.
With regard to the point made by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) at the conclusion of his remarks, that is a matter which I hope the Prime Minister will deal with at the proper time and in- the proper place. I do not think we can properly discuss the clauses of the bill on the motion for second reading.

Mr. Speaker, the measure before the house meets with the unqualified approval of the members of the Social Credit group. We entertain very much the same ideas as have already been expressed by the leaders of the two other opposition groups in the house. To emphasize the truth of what was said by each of those leaders, it is only necessary to point out that we are faced with problems the like of which have never before impressed themselves upon the minds of men.
In addition to our need to maintain the most harmonious and cooperative relations with the sister states of the great British empire and commonwealth; in addition to our need to have the most cordial fellowship with the United States; in addition to our need to extend the hand of good fellowship and good neighbourliness to all nations of the world who are kindly disposed-in addition to all these we have certain special problems that face us in this age.
The first, whic-h. should be impressed on all of us in all countries, is the need of developing a technique of distribution among nations. Very little is said about this matter, which is one of the greatest causes for anxiety that I see on the horizon to-day. The cause of the present troubles in the world is fundamentally the inability to distribute the goods of the
world from nation to nation. That was fundamentally the cause of the last war and of the first world war as well. Instead of our talking about that cause and trying to remedy it, it seems to me that the nations of the world and the members of this house are talking about everything else. In the existence of that cause there is occasion for alarm.
It seems to me that the Department of External Affairs of Canada will have to study this whole matter of international distribution with the utmost care and formulate a solution very different from anything the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has ever mentioned in all his public utterances outside or inside this house. In order to emphasize that fact I should like to point out one thing which has developed during the war.
We have built at Sarnia a great rubber plant at a cost, I understand, of 851,000,000. The result of that splendid experiment and achievement is that we now are independent of all the world with respect to rubber. But in developing our own rubber supply we have put out of employment 100,000 people in, the various countries that used to supply us with rubber. The question must arise in the mind of every thoughtful man: what is going to happen to those 100,000 people? Undoubtedly we were sound in developing our rubber supply, and it may easily be argued that we have no responsibility whatsoever for the welfare of those 100,000 people. But in this age, when we might be plunged into a war because of the unhappiness of certain peoples, we must assume a measure of responsibility for the welfare of those people. The nations of the world are developing towards economic nationalism, as has been pointed out two or three times already in debates in this house; and the more nearly they develop towards that state of affairs the more serious this problem becomes. There are nations-Canada and the United States, for instance-so fortunately situated in the extent and great variety of their resources as to be able in large measure to support themselves, but there are other nations whose resources are so meagre, and so one-sided, shall I say, that they cannot be self-sustaining. This state of affairs, alone, which is an exceedingly serious one, could occupy the Department of External Affairs pretty well night and day for enough years at least to enable them to reach a solution of the problem, which they can suggest to our fellow nations as they meet them.
There is another matter which requires special care at this time. During the Bretton Woods debate I pointed out that commercial rivalries and commercial warfare are far more

External Affairs

dangerous than they have ever been in the whole previous history of the world. I have no desire to offend anyone, but let me mention frankly one nation, our great, friendly respected and honoured neighbour, the United States. Because of her tremendous resources and wealth and her vast productive potential, the United States is capable of penetrating the markets of almost any nation in the world and displacing, the products of the industries of those nations, throwing their people into the ranks of the unemployed and generally wrecking their economy. If the people of the United States so desired, having upset the trade balance between themselves and any other nation in the world, with the exception of Russia perhaps, they could acquire the fixed assets of that nation and virtually render it impossible for her to conduct a free and independent life. Somehow or other the nations of the world must discover a means of offsetting the great danger of economic warfare. I am quite disheartened sometimes when I reflect on how few members of this house ever give any attention whatsoever to this important matter. Yet it is one of the major causes of war, and always has been. It was one of the major causes of the last war.
Another serious problem which bulks large upon the horizon is the need for safeguarding national sovereignty. To me there is a situation in our house which is quite fantastic. May I illustrate it by what happened within the last few minutes. The member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was speaking of our being independent of Britain, and I believe it was the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) who broke out with applause for that statement and said "hear, hear."

understanding to-day of the fundamental causes of international discord than I believe has ever been had by any nation in the past. We have to bo kept fully informed upon all matters pertaining to problems of the kind, and we have to have men in our external affairs department who are not burdened with any other matters except these, in order that they may have the mature judgment and the utmost of diplomatic skill to enable Canada to play her part in guaranteeing not only her own security and safety but the security and safety of the rest of mankind.

While the government
was in office, excluding the years 1930 to 1935. Since 1921, this country has emerged as one of the leading middle powers of the world. A former prime minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, during the first world war, under whom both Canada and the Department of External Affairs entered a new phase, occupied at that important period in the history of1 the world not only the post of prime minister but that of minister of external affairs. From 1921 to 1930 and from 1930 to the present time, Canada has developed from the position of a selfgoverning dominion to the full status of an equal and powerful nation among all the other nations of the commonwealth and nations of the world.
One would of course be exaggerating to attribute that remarkable development of our national life as a member in the family of states solely to one man; that I do not propose to do. But the undoubted fact is that the experience, the devotion and the farsightedness of the present Prime Minister of Canada have made him, as no other man in this country now is, equipped at this particularly difficult period in history to be not only Prime Minister of Canada but to act in the capacity-I trust, for some time to come as minister of external affairs. Reference has been made to the fact by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who graciously acknowledged the great record of achievement of the present leader of the house as Prime Minister and minister of external affairs, that we have in the Department of External Affairs one of the best manned departments in the government of Canada. As he said, at the international gatherings which he has attended and at the four which I have attended, the members of that department hold their own with any corresponding group from any other country. That did not arise simply by chance; it arose because of the determination of the minister in charge of that particular department to see to it that it was manned by the best men and women we could get from Canada into that particular branch of the public service. I believe that in discussing this measure the least we can do, not only on this but as well on the other side of the house, regardless of our political affiliations, is to acknowledge what Canada owes to the present Prime Minister in his capacity of Secretary of State for External Affairs.
It is said that the time has come, not only that we should have a separate minister but that the nomination of that minister should be made forthwith. I would respectfully point out that at the present time the Minister of External Affairs in South Africa is the Right Hon. Jan Smuts, the Prime Minister of that country. The Right Hon. Peter Fraser, as Prime Minister of New Zealand, still represents his country at important international gatherings such as that at San Francisco and at the first general assembly in London of the united nations. But it is to be noted that within five years Australia has had no less than three different prime ministers, one of whom was quite ill; one on his own admission did not expect to be able to hold the post of prime minister very long, and it may be presumed that in that great country there

There is another aspect, Mr. Speaker, which I think the house and the country will not overlook at this time, because this matter is one of tremendous importance. During the war important conferences were held at Quebec and, recently, at Washington. Mr. Churchill and Mr. Roosevelt conferred on extremely important matters affecting not only the welfare of the united nations but that of the post-war world. On two occasions these conferences were held at Quebec. The Prime Minister, representing Canada, participated in many of these discussions. To-day he is perhaps the only living man at the head of a government who has had constant contact with these two great world leaders, one of whom is no longer living and the other no longer in power. The Prime Minister of Canada is the only contact of continuity, from one point of view, with respect to many of the matters discussed and decided at those important meetings. More important still was the recent conference at Washington with respect to the important scientific discovery of atomic energy. The present Prime Minister of Canada, conferring as he did with Mr. Truman, the President of the United States, and Mr. Attlee, the Prime Minister of Great Britain, in the light of his discussions at Quebec and in the light of his great experience during the war, being the sole survivor of that trio, undoubtedly was able to contribute immeasurably to the important discussions on atomic energy. And I do not think I am

being indiscreet when I say I am sure the present Prime Minister of Great Britain would be the first to acknowledge, as he has said in my presence on two occasions within the past three months, when he said: "It is fortunate for the world that at this time we have at the head of certain governments men of the experience and prestige of the present Prime Minister of Canada and the Prime Minister of South Africa."
So at this time I rise not only in respect of a matter that has to do with the welfare of our country and the pursuit of its foreign policy, but to pay tribute to a distinguished member of this house, a great prime minister in war and a great prime minister in peace, and one of the most experienced and mature minds, in the field of international relations, to be found in any country in the world at the present time.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) has spoken very well about the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), but I regret to say that in some respects he has stolen my speech. I always listen to him with great pleasure, as I do to the other hon. members who have spoken. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydion) spoke as a jurist who might be sitting on an international court somewhere in Europe. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) spoke as a good Canadian, and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) made a delightful speech in his own way.
Of course opinions are free. This bill is very short, but it covers a very wide field. It covers the whole external policy of Canada. The question is not so much that of changing the incumbent of the post, though the Prime Minister knows what personal regard and admiration I have for him. The question is whether or not Canada will be what it has been described as being among the nations of the world. We hear the finest speeches about the role of Canada, about Canada being a great nation. I agree with that, but I always disagree with the sordid idea of making Canada in the first place a small nation and afterward making Canada a middle nation or middle power, adding "power" to "middle" to deceive the universe about the real role of Canada. Canada has been minimized by the three big powers who want to control the destinies of the world, but who are unable, unqualified and incompetent to do so. They are only troublemakers who come to secret arrangements on other things, arrangements which they are ashamed to publicize. They are incompetent to stop the evil menace they have started.
Here we are with Canada being described as one of the great nations of the world. I agree that Canada should be a great nation, that it should be considered as such and should be invited to participate when decisions are made. Canada was not elected to the security council; we had to take it for granted1 that what' was decided by the representatives of the three big nations was good for us. "Take that cure; it is good for you, my boy. Take your medicine; it is good for you. Take that spanking; it is good for you. That is good for you. Pay for us; it is good for you. Give to us; it ia good for you." We have to receive the prescription for our external policy from other nations, and here we come to the abandonment of part of sovereignity, which means that the Canadian people, those living within this country, will have no complete freedom and no liberty if our country has none. I regret that a gentleman with the intelligence of the former leader of the Social Credit group should deny freedom of speech to the point of being surprised when a member of parliament says he wants this country to be free from England as well as free from the United States.

speechtext:
Every bit of it. I must qualify what I have said regarding the independence of this country. I do not mean that this country must be independent of the people of Great Britain and of the United States, not at all. What I wish to qualify in my former statement is that in my humble view Canada should be independent of all those who are the official representatives of any other country, France, England, The Netherlands, China and so forth, to make her own decisions regarding our external policy, regarding the relations of Canada with other nations. That, is why I find that I cannot subscribe to the united nations organization. Perhaps I am ahead of my time; but when we see the trouble that is existing throughout the world to-day and when we read column after column and page after page of the papers telling us of the intrigues that have been taking .place in New York and in all other places where there have been UNO conferences, are we to be governed by those people whom we do not know? I asked the question the other day. If I were in the United States I would favour Governor Dewey of the state of New York and I would vote Republican. If I were in England I would be very much embarrassed to decide between the two main parties, now that the Liberal party is dead in England. In Russia I would not be at liberty to express any opinion. It is these three big countries that rule the world now. It is the labour government in England; it is the democratic party in the United States and it is the government of Soyiet Russia joined together. Sometimes they do not agree among themselves in sharing the spoils but they dictate as to what we shall do. I am against it. I believe in the sovereignty of Canada, in the complete and full sovereignty of Canada, just as much as I believe in the freedom and liberty of the Canadian citizen, if one man is ever to be so named officially. I believe in liberty, and I cannot conceive how citizens of any country could be free when the country itself is under the yoke of other nations. This I cannot subscribe to.
We have representatives throughout the world. Here in Canada we are young; we are childish, we are naive; we are credulous; we talk of diplomats. They are just commercial agents. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) said it last year or the year before. The high commissioner for Great 
Britain is only a commercial agent; so are our high commissioners. They come under the Secretary of State for External Affairs. They should be under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have high regard for our high commissioners, especially for one of them whom I know very well. He is a former judge, my old friend, Mr. Justice Davis, high commissioner for Canada in Australia. What has he to do except looking after commercial interests over there? I admit that on certain occasions the high commissioner for Canada to Great Britain has something else to do. He is known as the go-between between the dominion government and His Majesty's government in England. That is a particular case, but all the others are there precisely to promote trade. They are there as consuls de luxe, a little above consuls general.
I said that we are naive. I take the Parliamentary Guide and I look at it. For a long time we had no ambassadors in this country. We had one high commissioner, but no others. We had several consuls. Well, these consuls were given official precedence as follows:
Ambassadors, foreign ministers and foreign consuls general accredited to Canada, though not .provided for in the table of precedence, are given a courtesy precedence, the ambassadors and ministers following immediately after the lieutenant .governors of the provinces, and the consuls general immediately after the prime ministers of the .provinces. The high commissioner and other representatives of the British commonwealth have been granted precedence immediately after tbe moderator of the Presbyterian church in Canada.
Sir, the gallery has been cleared of members' friends and relations to make place for the so-called diplomats. There is no one in the gallery facing the chair and very few people in the gallery to your left. These galleries were held in petto for the so-called diplomats and they do not even come to hear the discussions on a bill of this importance. It would have been beneficial to listen not to my remarks, but to those which have been made so ably by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and by the former leader of the opposition and the other hon gentlemen who have spoken; but the so-called diplomats shine by their absence to-day.
What is the present position of Canada with regard to trade, for instance? As high commissioners' duty is only to look after trade and as they come under the Secretary of State for External Affairs, it is incumbent upon them to be completely independent of the official representatives of any other country, including Great Britain, the United States, and the part of the world to which

External Affairs
they are assigned to perform their duty. Their duty is not to promote English trade, United States trade or Chinese trade; their duty is to promote Canadian trade and they should be independent of all these agencies. They should not be under the tutelage of the ambassadors of the United Kingdom, they should be independent of the high commissioners, independent of the consuls of Great Britain. Why? Because if there is the least difficulty respecting trade they must not look after the interests of any other country; they must look first after the interests of Canada. That is my point of view with regard to the usefulness of high commissioners and consuls general. - I think there is only one in the United States at the present time - and all the commercial attaches that we have throughout the world. What can we expect with regard to trade if these gentlemen have to give obedience to any English gentleman who is there, have to report to him or have to seek his advice?
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was perfectly right when he said that we should have a Canadian policy applied to trade. I remember distinctly when a well-known imperialist who was the former member for York-Sunbury, Mr. Hanson, and a former leader of the opposition in this house was sitting here and I said to him that perhaps it was not the time for Canada to be politically independent of the United Kingdom. I said that during the war, but I also said on the same occasion that Canada should be economically independent of Great Britain. I said that if the time ever came to choose between the interest of Great Britain and any other country, France as well as any other, on the one hand and that of Canada on the other, our choice should unquestionably be Canada. I will choose Canada, and I shall try to help my fellow-Canadians. That is the byword that should be given to all the men who come under the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Our only hope, our only life-preserver to prevent Canada from falling into bankruptcy is a resumption of our prewar trade with all the nations of the world, not by way of gift, not by the Santa Claus policy, but by actually receiving payments for what we sell them. That is my point of view; I may be wrong. But I believe that in the event of any discussion, or in the event of a division of opinion, all the men under the Secretary of State for External Affairs, or under the Minister of Trade and Commerce - all those who represent Canadian interests overseas must be one to defend and promote Canadian interests and trade, as well as any other matters.
We hear some say the Prime Minister is a great man. I believe so. I believe his name will be written in golden letters in the annals of Canada as a man who wanted his country to be one of the greatest in the world, a man who has acquired world-wide fame, one of the most able conciliators to be found in diplomatic circles.
I agree with all that. And that is precisely why I was so much disappointed and my heart was so full of sorrow when I thought of the Big Three who were meeting together, and talking so psst, psst, psst-but who did not invite the Prime Minister of Canada, so as to have the benefit of his wisdom and vision and perhaps save the situation.
The right hon. gentleman has the prestige of a quarter of a century or more as Prime Minister of Canada. He has the knowledge of the past, and the knowledge of great men of the past. He knows that, although it may be a matter of regret to all, when he thinks he has performed his duty, he may retire.
But now he is opening the way for the creation of another department. Everybody is enthusiastic for it. Well, I know there are some able men in the cabinet, men for whom I have deep respect. But that is not enough. If we want Canada to be respected through and through by the other nations of the world, then the position of Secretary of State for External Affairs must be considered by the government of this country as the most important in the interests of Canada. The man who will be in charge of that department must have enough prestige to have influence within the cabinet, and to impose Canadian views upon his colleagues when they are about to jump the fence because of sentimentality.
If the Prime Minister made a success of his term as Secretary of State for External Affairs it was precisely because he was Prime Minister of Canada. Without his learning, without his sagacity, without his shrewdness, or his experience, and had he not had the prestige of Prime Minister of a country I consider the greatest in the world, he would not have succeeded half as well.
Therefore we must be cautious. It is not a matter of the Prime Minister's letting anyone get into his shoes as Secretary of State for External Affairs-although I know there are some able ministers. The point is that the next Secretary of State for External Affairs in Canada shall at the same time be the Prime Minister, in spite of this legislation, so that he may control the destinies of this country throughout the world. It will be a hard fight. It will no longer be a matter of conciliation. Rather it will be one of facing interests that are ready to do anything to control the trade of the world, the riches of
External Afjairs

the world, the natural resources of the world. The Secretary of State for External Affairs will have to watch all those racketeers in international finance who want to control all we have in this country, and all there is in the world. A man will need the highest of all qualities in order to defend our birthright and to protect our interests. He shall not be governed by sentimentality; rather he shall be governed by a word which has been deprecated-he shall be governed by patriotism. For a time everyone would raise his shoulders when patriotism was mentioned, when it was called nationalism. Now the word has changed; it is called isolationism. Am I an isolationist if I want my country to prosper, if I want my country to be the greatest in the world? I am not an isolationist. I am a patriot, and I want Canada to be what she is described to be.
Otherwise let us speak no more about the greatness of Canada. Let us say that we are a colony, but we have no reason to be impressed by our creditors from other nations who come here, look at us from the galleries and say, "Those are the people who make the gifts; how silly they look!" I do not say that they use that expression, but we read that in their eyes.
Let us not be concerned about them. Let us have that dignity that is required of all those who are at the helm of all nations. Let us think of the present time and of the future; let us not be impressed by anyone from out- [DOT] side. Let us think first of the citizens of our own country. Let us think first of our country-and that does not mean that we are unwilling to deal with any other nation. But when we do so, it will be done in the interests of Canada and for the protection of our fellow citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house is to amend the Department of External Affairs Act, which was passed in 1927. The amendment is not as simple as it looks, because there are many principles involved.
While I would speak with great respect about the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and about the hard work he and his officials have done in the department, and while I have respect for his wide experience, I would offer some constructive objections to the proposed policy.
While I cannot speak with authority respecting the policy of this party, and would speak only as a private member, might I say that our policy has been consistent. Notwithstanding what has been said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, the hope of the world is that France and Great Britain will work together.

I do not wish to discuss external affairs at this time, and shall be content only to speak concerning the principle involved in the bill. It must be remembered that the policy of the [DOT] mother country is to restore France to the great nation she has always been in the past. I hope our friends from Quebec will not forget that.
Speaking back in 1938, and paying tribute to what the Prime Minister had done, I said:
Under our constitutional practice, however, as the Prime Minister is 'aware, seeing that he has had a great deal of experience in diplomatic -affairs, it is the duty of parliament to inquire into estimates such as those we have before us tp-day.
I pointed out that on the government of the day rests the responsibility for the conduct of external affairs, and not on the opposition. We as an opposition should not act as life-preservers for the government because on the government of the day as long as they are the government of the day is the onus and responsibility for the conduct of Canada's external affairs. We are spending on this Department of External Affairs now a total of four and one-third million dollars.
The question arises as to the cause and effect of the proposed amendment. The external affairs policy to-day is totally different from what it was in 1927 when this statute which it is now proposed to amend was passed. After all is said and done, external affairs, as a great textbook writer, Walter Lippmann, said, should be largely a matter of what one might call a chartered accountant's policy by which you strike a balance sheet of assets and liabilities and decide as a country what commitments you have to meet and what you will be able to do with them in the event of war. Thai is a very good definition.
As I see it, the foreign policy of this country should be based on two principles. It will be remembered that when the proposal to appoint parliamentary assistants was up a couple of years ago I stated that I did not believe in the principle, although I understand it has worked out very well in some departments. I know the Prime Minister has a heavy load to carry in this particular department, and at that time it was suggested that a parliamentary assistant should fill this office instead of a minister of the crown. That policy was adopted with regard to other departments.
I do not think it is in the interest of responsible government that representatives of the opposition parties should be sent abroad on external affairs missions to represent the government. I am not objecting merely to spending money and I always believe it is a

External Affairs
good thing for members of parliament to travel. The principle was adopted of sending these deputations abroad a few years ago to the league. First, I think the Secretary of State was a delegate once and now it is continued on foreign affairs. The government of the day must accept responsibility alone for foreign affairs.
There are a great many people in this country who are becoming alarmed at the way our foreign affairs are being conducted. They are comparing the principles which were laid down by the government and by others before this war with those being laid down to-day. In 1938 I suggested to the Prime Minister of the day that he should avail himself of the facilities of the radio, and I believe he did that a little later on. On March 24, 1938, I proposed that to the Prime Minister and, as I say, that practice was carried out during the war. If that had been done in connection with external affairs I do not think there would be the criticism there has been. I suggest to the Prime Minister that there should be an empire conference of the dominions on cooperation and coordination if this amendment is passed. This has been suggested for many years and it is the only way of settling these problems. That should be done instead of sending abroad these deputations to which I have referred. There should be a meeting of the dominions to lay down a common, after the war, empire policy. As has been said by President Poincaire of France, we are the hardest country in the world with which to make a treaty, as Britain always spoke with so many divergent views.
I object to the amendment because the Department of External Affairs of to-day is not the same as the department that was set up under the act of 1927. It has been expanded, and we are assuming responsibility which it was never intended the department should take under responsible government. I have looked into this matter for a long time. We are a country of only 10,500,000 people and we are spending $4,300,000 on this particular department. When I see the deviations which have been made from the statute of 1927 in our foreign policy I become alarmed and many thoughtful people are becoming alarmed over what is going to happen to our policy.
In conclusion, I wish to say that a great many thoughtful people believe that this work could be carried out by a parliamentary assistant. Are we to have a foreign minister like the old country? I have referred to the fact that all Britain's foreign ministers were trained men, and also their permanent officials on diplomacy, such as Spring-Rice and Lindsay at
Washington. If the Prime Minister wants this particular bill to pass, aid very well and good, but I suggest that the province of Ontario should receive some consideration for such a new minister, especially the Toronto district, which has not had a cabinet minister since the present government came into office, and even long before that.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
