speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a word before second reading is given. First of all, may I say that my reason for introducing this bill has been to further not only the wishes of many hon. gentlemen opposite but my own wishes as well. I think I have made it clear from time to time that I was not over-anxious to carry the extra burdens of the Department of External Affairs in addition to those of the Prime Minister. I certainly would not be carrying both portfolios at the present time if it were not that the questions which are uppermost in this and other countries to-day are for the most part international questions which call for as much in the wray of experience and knowledge as it is possible for one to command, and also for the fact that the two departments, the department of the Prime Minister and that of the Secretary of State for External Affairs have been so interlocked for the past thirty or forty years that the separation of those two departments at a given moment is not something that can be very readily brought about.
Let me say a word first in regard to the latter point. I know that hon. gentlemen are anxious to know why it is, being desirous of being relieved of certain burdens, one has not found it possible to find that relief up to the present time. In that connection I have to explain the position of the Prime Minister when he comes into office as contrasted with that of other ministers of the crown. As hon. gentlemen know, when a minister other than the Prime Minister assumes a portfolio he goes into a department of state which is already thoroughly organized and has been organized for years past. His department has a deputy head; it has a secretary; it has its various branches; it has its staff of civil servants who know all the aspects of the work of the department and who possess the accumulated knowledge and information of which the department has become the repository over many years.
When the Prime Minister assumes offices he enters what to all intents and purposes is an all but completely empty office. If he is fortunate enough to have had them, he takes with him one or two secretaries who have served him in his capacity as leader of the opposition if he comes into office after having

External Affairs

been the leader of the opposition. Otherwise he has no officers whatever in his department until he has had an opportunity to organize the Prime Minister's office. He has no deputy head; he has no secretary of his department as such; he has no leading officials as such. There may be a few stenographers and typists and possibly a few members of the service who have had to do with the filing of communications. He has to ask himself immediately whether those particular officials who have been serving political opponents are the ones whom he wishes to have continue in the office with him having regard to all the intimate affairs of government with which the Prime Minister finds he is confronted. I am happy to say that I have found that it was not necessary to change these members of the service to any extent, and one of the reasons is that they have been so few in number.
The one criticism of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) with regard to this present step was that it was not taken two or three years ago. ff the measure is to be criticized for coming so late, my criticism would be that it did npt come many years ago, and in particular that it did not come at the time when his leader, the then Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, was prime minister of Canada and also secretary of state for external affairs. I am wholly right, I believe, when f say that when Lord Bennett became prime minister he had previously entertained the view that it would be desirable to separate the two offices, but he had been in office for only a very short time before he expressed quite frankly the view that it would not be wise to separate the two offices. He found that the Department of External Affairs was in many important particulars concerned with the work that the Prime Minister's office would have to undertake in connection with very many of . the questions that came up, and throughout the five years that he was in office he continued to hold the two positions. If those positions had been separated during the term of Mr. Bennett's prime ministership of this country it would have meant that we would have had a separate minister of external affairs in 1935. I mention 1935 as a significant date because in the years immediately following, as all hon. members know, the question of foreign relations became a matter of grave concern not only for a secretary of state for external affairs but very much a matter of deep concern to the prime minister. Those were the years when we were approaching the possibility of war in Europe, and it fell to my lot to have the administration of both 
positions at that time. I should have found it perilous and indeed impossible to have separated those two positions at that particular time, and had they been separated I am sure I am quite right when I say that once we came to the period of the war, it would have been almost imperative for the Prime Minister to hold the position of Secretary of State for External Affairs as well as the office of Prime Minister. There would otherwise have been duplication of the work all the way through with resulting confusion. Through the period of the war the work of the two departments became necessarily more intertwined than ever. May I say to hon. members of the house that, so far as the Prime Minister's office to-day is concerned nearly all the officials on whom he relies in the Prime Minister's office have been seconded to that office from the Department of External Affairs. It has been necessary to have experienced officials. Experienced officials, with like qualifications, were not to be found in any other department of government or outside the government service. More than that, let me say in passing, there can be no better field of training for the officials of the Department of External Affairs than the Prime Minister's office. I think it is very desirable, when these departments are separated, as I hope they will be before very long, that some members of the Department of External Affairs should continue to serve in the Prime Minister's office and to obtain, while there, all the knowledge they possibly can on questions that are all-important in government. It is the best school of training for the young men and women who are to be entrusted with the larger responsibility, of later filling great positions and representing our country in other lands.
And so it is that if these offices were separated immediately a good deal of care would have to be exercised in untwining the threads that have formed so complete a strand uniting thq two offices. If it were not for that difficulty I can assure hon. members that the severance would have been made some considerable time before this. As an illustration. of how much this is the case I might mention that at the present time, so far as the Prime Minister's office is concerned, all the accounting of that office and practically all its business administration is managed from the Department of External Affairs and has been so managed since 1912.
I would remind hon. members that when the act creating the Department of External Affairs was introduced by Sir Robert Borden in 1912, it provided:

External Affairs
The member of the King's Privy Council for Canada holding the recognized position of First Minister shall be the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and in this act he is hereunder referred to as "the minister."
Sir Robert Borden did not insert that clause without having very strong and good reasons at the time for so doing, and as I have pointed out, Lord Bennett, when he was prime minister, allowed that clause to remain in the act, having the very best of reasons for feeling it was essential that the Department of External Affairs should be so closely united with the Prime Minister's office. As I have just said, I have found, particularly through the years of war, and, indeed, in no less degree since, that it was imperative that the Prime Minister should have the closest possible contact with the officials of the external affairs department, thus bringing him in immediate touch, as he only could come in immediate touch, with those who were representing Canada in all the different countries in which we have missions, and also all who were representing Canada at important international gatherings.
I pause for a moment to refer lion, members to the estimates as they have been presented to this house for the present year. Hon. members will see in a moment to what an extent much of the business that would otherwise have to be separately provided for in the Prime Minister's estimates is to-day provided for in the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. In this year's estimates for 1946-47 there is provided for the Prime Minister's office a total of $78,073, and for the Department of External Affairs, $2,436,325. That speaks for itself of the extent to which these two departments have become interlocked, and that over a period of thirty-four years. I want the house to understand this very clearly because some people may think that I am desirous of holding on to more in the way of administration than in fact I desire to do. A main reason, I wish to repeat, why a complete division of the two departments had not been made before this is that it will involve, when finally made, a very considerable readjustment of what will have to be provided in connection with the Prime Minister's office and also changes of importance in the Department of External Affairs as well.
I appreciate the solicitude of hon. gentlemen opposite for my health and strength and all the rest of it that on occasions they have been kind enough to express. But I take all that with a grain of salt. I must say, I ask myself, just why do they want me out of this office? If I were not of some value to
the country as head of the Department of External Affairs, I am certain they would be glad to see me stay there, and they would not be asking me to retire as quickly as possible. As I say, I question a little what some of them, at least, may have in mind, but I agree with them that as soon as matters can be properly arranged with due regard to the public interest, it is desirable that the two departments should be separated.
But I come then to the question of whether at this particular moment it is best to make that change. The first step is being taken now. It is a wholly necessary step in that we are removing what up to this time has been at the instance of parliament a bar to anyone other than the Prime Minister * holding that office. I am hopeful that very shortly another step may be taken, though I cannot at the .moment say just how soon. That., I know, is the main question in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite, how soon are we going to get this man out of that particular position? I wish I could satisfy my hon. friend, the member for Peel on that, but he will just have to wait and see in regard to that, as to much else. May I remind my hon. friend, when he undertakes to tell me what should be done in the Department of External Affairs, that I have had experience in that department which runs nearly to twenty years. Such experience as he has had in international affairs has resulted,
I think, from my own act in appointing him as a delegate to the United Nations conference on international organization at San Francisco, also a member of the Canadian delegation to the preparatory commission of the united nations, and still later as an alternate delegate of the first session of the general assembly of the united nations. I am glad to see that he has profited somewhat by that experience. But let me tell him that twenty years experience with international affairs is worth a great deal more than one year, or a few months, and that if he had had a little wider experience I think he might have been somewhat more cautious in suggesting that the changes he proposes should be made at this particular moment.
I ask myself this question: with what countries has Canada very important relations at the present time? First of all there are our relations with the United Kingdom and other parts of the British commonwealth; there are our relations with the United States, with France, with China, and with Russia. This house knows that the problems we have in all these relationships have not grown up in the last few days, or weeks, or years; they have come into being over the years, and with
63260-32i
External Affairs

respect to them, wide knowledge and information is a very great asset in reaching highly important decisions. The movement'of international affairs is so rapid in these days that unless one has some of the direct knowledge of the background out of which these situations have sprung it would be next to impossible with respect to many of them to make with any sense of security the decisions which are essential if the proper steps are to be taken. I shall give but one example of what I mean. I ask the house this question: supposing I were to resign to-morrow the position of Secretary of State for External Affairs, what would the reaction be in Russia to that resignation? Would it be represented that I still commanded the confidence of the parliament and people of Canada in international affairs, or would it be represented that, having taken the position which I have taken in the interests of this country, this House of Commons and the people of Canada hold a very different view with respect to the manner in which I have discharged my responsibilities? That is something which has not occurred to my hon. friend. But I tell him that considerations of the kind in international relations are vital in reaching decisions as to what particular moment it is best for changes to be made.
Reference has been made, very kindly, oh the part of my colleague the Secretary of State. (Mr. Martin) and the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) to what it may mean at some international gatherings at this time to have the experience of such a person - such a great leader-as Jan Smuts, who holds the position of Minister of External Affairs as well as Prime Minister and whose influence at these gatherings arises out of the great part which he has taken in international affairs over the years. It is not for me to say whether or not a new minister of external affairs coming into office to-morrow would be able, in the critical situations which have to be dealt with at some of the international gatherings which are to take place this year, to render, perhaps, the same service to Canada as one who has known at first hand the international situation as it has grown up over the years. As has been referred to this afternoon I have had -and I am very proud of it, and I believe it is an asset of national value-a very close and intimate association with both Mr. Churchill when he was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and with the late President Roosevelt of the United States. Very few men living to-day know what was in the minds of . these men when certain decisions were made, as well as I do myself; and of some of these

decisions, may I say, I think I have of those who are in office to-day, an almost exclusive knowledge. I say this in no boasting spirit but I know the value of authority in some things when one is speaking at international gatherings, and I know also the value of personal acquaintance and friendship with leading men in different parts of the world, and of having had what grows out of such an intimate association in years like those of the recent past.
I want to say this to my hon. friends opposite: I am prepared to accept from them as much in the way of advice as they may wish to tender and to consider it very carefully. But there is one group of gentlemen to whose advice and counsel and opinion I must give even more attention than to theirs, and that is, the colleagues who sit with me in the government, and the hon. members who through many years have been my loyal supporters in this House of Commons. When it comes to the matter of the responsibility of government for foreign affairs in times like the present one's colleagues have to be consulted, their views taken into consideration and their wishes considered as well as one's own. I have not found among my colleagues thus far a desire that I should give up this particular post at, this particular time, nor have I found that wish among members of my party.
After all, it is our responsibility to govern. Having been sent here for that purpose, having been sent here, as the Secretary of State, without possibility of any contradiction, said, by the Canadian people because they believed that this particular government was best qualified to deal with external affairs at a time which was very critical in the world, that responsibility is something which in fact I have to recognize in my obligation to the people of Canada.
I say these things that hon. members may realize that it is not all just as easy to bring about a change as they themselves may think. I am anxious to lighten the load in as many directions as I can. Thank God, I have around me ministers who are taking more of it from my shoulders day by day. It might appear that I am carrying a great deal of the load. I have to take the responsibility for what is said and done, but if hon. members will notice how matters related to external affairs have been dealt with in considerable part by one minister after the other they will realize that the burden of the Department of External Affairs is not wholly on the shoulders of any one man, but is shared by a large part of [he ministry.

External Affairs
That I say simply to clear up what my hon. friend seems most concerned about, namely as to when I am to get out of this particular position. May I say what I have in mind is that I know hon. members are very anxious to discuss external affairs at an early stage of the session; also that they are anxious to have the estimates of the Department of External Affairs referred at any stage to the committee on external affairs. I had thought that if it suited the convenience of the house I might try to bring forward the debate on external affairs within another fortnight, and as soon as the house had passed an item, refer the estimates at once to a committee, where they might be gone into thoroughly. But I must say to my hon. friend that I do not think it would be in his interests, in the interests of this house or in the interests of this country for me to attempt within the next few weeks to have one of my colleagues appointed as Secretary of State for External Affairs and put upon his' shoulders the responsibility of conducting the first discussion and the main discussion we shall have on external affairs.

I have been giving consideration to it. There may be some technical advantage in further amending the act respecting the Department of External Affairs, but I really think what is now proposed is quite sufficient, for the reason that the original bill itself provided for a Secretary of State for External Affairs. Section
2	of that bill is as follows:
There, shall be a department of the government of Canada to be called the Department of External Affairs, over which the Secretary of State for External Affairs shall preside.
That makes provision - for a secretary of state to preside over a Department of External Affairs. Then the Salaries Act provides:
These salaries of the following ministers, members of the King's privy council for Canada, shall be as follows, that is to say:
The Secretary of State for External Affairs.

So that S10,000 is voted for the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the act defines him as a minister. It seems to me, therefore, that all that is necessary to meet the situation to which my hon. friend has referred is fully covered. The act makes provision for the department; it makes provision for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to be at the head of the department; another act defines him as a minister; and wherever the word "minister" is referred to in this act the minister would be the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
If I might just ask a question, because I heard this comment, I understand that the salary provision becomes operative only if a separate minister is appointed for the department.

speechtext: That is right. The salary has been there for the last two years. I made the suggestion that it should be included a couple of years ago, hoping someone other than myself would get it; it will be there when a new minister is appointed.

With due respect to what the right hon. Prime Minister has said I might point out one further matter. That is, while I appreciate his statement, it is normal in an act setting up a department to provide for the appointment of a minister who shall preside over that department; and as the act would now stand no such provision is made. So that I would ask, for instance, under what authority would the Secretary of State for External Affairs be appointed?

speechtext:
The act says:
There shall be .a department of the government of Canada to be called the Department of External Affairs, over which the Secretary of State for External Affairs shall preside.
I am afraid I do not quite catch my hon. friend's objection. Does he feel that this is not enough?

It is a matter of statutory form, if you wish. I am merely pointing out that the clause says, "over which the secretary of state shall preside," but still we have no provision for the appointment of a Secretary of State for External Affairs. It is normal to provide that the minister shall be appointed under the great seal, and shall hold office, and so on, and I merely point out that there is this exception. It is a small matter, but we have asked if the Prime Minister would be willing to introduce an amendment. I drafted a section after the hon. member for Peel spoke. I do not know whether this might meet the situation. There shall be a department of the government of Canada to be called the Department of External Affairs, over which a minister of the crown .to be known as the Secretary of State for External Affaire and hereafter referred to as "the minister" shall preside.
If that is acceptable to my hon. friends opposite I would be happy to have it moved.
If the Prime Minister still occupies the position of Secretary of State for External Affairs there will be no extra expense. If a new minister is appointed the only extra expense will be his salary?

There is no provision for a staff for the Prime Minister. The staff of the Prime Minister for the most part are members of the Department of External Affairs who are seconded to the Prime Minister's office. There are other changes which do not come to mind at the moment but which are far-reaching. If there had been time to work out that division quickly within the last few months I would have been only too happy to do so, but I think it will take some short time to have it properly worked out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APRIL 10 AS JACK MINER NATIONAL WILD LIFE DAY

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, March 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacNicol for the second reading of bill No. 2, respecting the Jack Miner National Wild Life Day.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APRIL 10 AS JACK MINER NATIONAL WILD LIFE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the second reading of bill No. 2, respecting Jack Miner national wild life day, has created an incident which is not only unusual but, I think, unique in the annals of this house. We are asked to commemorate the life of a citizen, and with it to identify him with his life's work.

National Wild Life Day
The speeches which have so far been heard are a worthy tribute to one who, in his lifetime, became known far and wide, and especially on this continent, for his great and valuable contribution to the knowledge of wild bird life. He began his life's work under circumstances very adverse, and sometimes under the sneering comment of his contemporaries which might have daunted a lesser man, but which only served to prove the indomitable spirit of this remarkable man.
It was given to few men, as it was given to Jack Miner, to receive in his lifetime the acclaim not only of those on this continent, but of those of many foreign lands. He exhibited the truth of that old and true saying, "Seest thou a man diligent in his business; he shall stand before kings."
Jack Miner in his life did stand among kings-kings of industry, political life and of every field of activity known to our civilization. But, above all, he stood a peer among his fellowmen-the common man. With it all he exhibited a robust Christianity which endeared him to those who believe in humanity and the eternal verities.
Full of years and his task showing promise of a prominence which his family are now endeavouring to consolidate, Jack Miner passed on, leaving his heritage to his immediate family, who are carrying on as he desired and as he would wish.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has told the house that there is a foundation called the Jack Miner foundation, which is carried on by the members of his family, and which is subject to the scrutiny of any who may wish to investigate. The hon. member for Davenport, because of his respect and admiration for Jack Miner, has brought this bill before the house. He was privileged to call Jack Miner his friend, and by this bill he has shown his desire to perpetuate that friendship and admiration in the form of the bill we are now discussing.
It is evident from the expressions from all sides of the house that the hon. member for Davenport has considerable support; and I am sure that as a recognition of the merits of Jack Miner, that support is universal on every side of the house. I should like to add that what I shall now say is not in opposition to or in any way to detract from the eminence of this great Canadian and great Christian gentleman. However, I should like the house to consider some angles of the bill which come to my mind.
The house will recall that last session I indicated, when my estimates were before the committee, and when the sum of $2,500 was being asked as a grant to the Jack Miner foundation, that I had received many letters
from hon. members on all sides of the house asking that the grant be restored to the amount at which it had formerly stood, namely $5,000. I stated at that time that when making up my estimates again I would endeavour to place the amount at $5,000, as before. I am now happy to say that I have been able to do so, and that hon. members will find in the estimates that the grant for the Jack Miner foundation is restored to its original sum of $5,000.
I am sure the house will agree that that estimate should pass, without discussion. Sometimes I think of the story of the old Quaker who was accosted by a friend who, in turn, was commiserating the condition of another friend. The old Quaker said, "Well, show us your sympathy", and he pulled out a pound note, saying, "There is the extent of my sympathy."
Perhaps the expression of the house in the grant of $5,000 is that form of expression which will be duly appreciated by those who will receive it. It may be that this bill, which is unusual _ and the first of its kind, would raise questions in the minds of hon. members as to the precedent about to be created. I do not know where we should stop, whether we should commemorate the life of any citizen in Canada in any field of activity. Shall we do so in the political field? If so, I can well understand that some hon. members might wish to commemorate the life of Sir John A. Macdonald, the father of Confederation, and whom, now that the partisan politics with which he was connected have passed away, we now view only as a great Canadian. If there were a suggestion to commemorate his life I am sure there are many Liberals on this side of the house who would recognize in Sir John A Macdonald not only a Conservative leader, but a leader of the Canadian people. I should imagine any suggestion of the kind I have mentioned would receive the acclaim of the country.
Then we might have a day set apart to commemorate the life of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, because, as hon. members will recall, he came into office as Prime Minister at a time when unity within the country was very much needed. We had not passed far from colonial days and he was faced with a task which might have daunted any lesser man. I think any fair-minded Canadian will agree, however, that the efforts made by Sir Wilfrid Laurierj while he was Prime Minister of .this country, tended to consolidate the nation to a point where he could visualize a united Canada.
I am sure that Conservatives or others throughout the country would recognize his worth as they recognize the worth of Sir John A.
National Wild Lije Day

Macdonald. They were leaders of Canada, and it might be fitting, in some minds, to have a day commemorating their memory.
Then, while we are still in the political field, there is Sir Robert Borden. Sir Robert Borden did noble work during the last war, as every one will recognize. But in my judgment he did still greater work when he became one of the proponents of the Statute of Westminster which consolidated Canada as an autonomous nation. These men in the political field have passed away, and I can understand that in the days to come there may be a day set aside to commemorate their memory.
I would expect also that many would like to set a day aside to commemorate the present leader of the House of Commons and Prime Minister of Canada. I know the day will come when party strife has left the minds of men and they will look only to the great events and achievements of his life and recognize fully, as with these others that I have mentioned, that he is one of the leaders of Canada, one of the makers of Canada. It may be that in the days to come there may also be set apart a day for Mackenzie King.
Leaving the political field, I have in mind one outstanding citizen of this country who has also passed away, namely, Doctor Saunders, the man who brought into being Marquis wheat. I know of no greater contribution that any citizen of this country could make than that of Doctor Saunders who brought into being our Marquis wheat. That wheat revolutionized farming in western Canada; it gave stability to the economy of our country. Only recently there has been evolved another wheat with qualities even greater than wheats that preceded it and they all stemmed from that product which he evolved, namely, Marquis wheat. If one is to consider a field of endeavour such as that of Doctor Saunders, one covering the whole of Canada, one having an effect upon all our lives, then it should be proper that he also should have a day of commemoration set apart such as is now being asked for in this bill for Jack Miner.
I have another great Canadian in mind, Doctor Banting, that great physician who evolved insulin. The effects of insulin are not only national, they are international. He devoted his life to the work of evolving that great medicine. In the pursuance of his profession and in an effort to assist in the war effort he lost his life on the shores of Newfoundland. One might also say that a day should be set aside to commemorate Doctor Banting because he was a benefactor of all mankind and was a citizen of Canada.

Recently I had an invitation to address the prospectors' and developers' association in Toronto. About one thousand men and women were gathered together there. I was asked to give these prospectors and developers an address, but before doing so I met the president of the association, Mrs. Viola McMillan, and she asked me to speak about and further, if necessary, the setting up of a miners' day in Canada. I felt then as I feel now that an innovation of that kind should not come from me. I thought that while it was a proper thing to have a miners' day for Canada in order that the people of this country may have an opportunity to gather in all the information they can about the development of our land, that suggestion should not come from me. The world looks upon Canada as the last great mining field on this continent and these people feel that something should be done to propagate and to extend their activities.
I felt that it was not something that I could give official sanction to, however I might feel as an individual. However, they had decided already that they were going to have a miners' day. They proposed to take the initiative and do the spade work to bring it into being. They set up a fund and many of those present contributed. I was impressed by a most colorful character who was there, whom many hon. members know, Jack Hammil, who there and then gave his cheque for $500 to help carry on an educational programme among these prospectors and developers and also throughout the provinces. These people will lay the foundation whereby miners' day might become identified with that industry and create interest in it which would be of value to the industry.
I notice that the explanatory notes to the bill state:
The purpose of this bill is to create public interest in the wild life of Canada and educate Canadians in the value thereof by setting aside a day when school teachers can stress in schools bird life, humane education, conservation, a day to judge bird-house contests . . .
The word "education" is brought into this, and it struck me that this bill should not be brought before this House of Commons at this time. My feeling is that the timing is not good. If there is a desire throughout Canada to have such a day, then it seems to me there ought to be some preparatory work done before such a bill is presented here. After all, we represent the dominion; we do not represent the provinces as provinces. The matter of education is wholly within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, and it might seem somewhat impertinent for the

National Wild Life Day
House of Commons to distinguish a day which would be related to the educational systems of the provinces when, indeed, they might be desirous of commemorating some of their own citizens. I would not be surprised if some of the provinces might desire that one or more of their eminent men should be commemorated in a form which this bill suggests.
At all events, my feeling is that this matter should not be brought before the House of Commons at this time. Communication should be entered into with the provinces to see what their viewpoint is. We are dealing with the provinces in the dominion-provincial conference, and it seems to me that we should not bring before them something which we propose to merge into their educational system and curricula without at least giving them an opportunity to say whether or not they desire it.
I did not wish to speak at any length upon this bill. I wish to make a suggestion to my hon. friend the member for Davenport, and I do so with some degree of timidity. He has proposed this bill with a desire to commemorate his friend and the friend of many in this house. During the discussion on this bill many hon. members have acclaimed the work of Jack Miner and of the foundation which now exists. I think the hon. member has done his duty, and he should now consider whether or not this is the proper time to bring a bill such as this before the house without some effort being made to find out the reaction of the provinces toward such a bill.
With the high regard that I have for the hon. member for Davenport I do not like to appear as being opposed to anything he may wish, but I would suggest to him that some communication should be had with the provinces and their points of view obtained. If, later on, the consensus is that the life of any citizen should be commemorated in this unique manner, then it might be brought before the house again. If the hon. member desires I shall be glad to assist him in obtaining expressions from the provinces of their points of View with regard to the bill.
I am hoping the hon. member will take this suggestion as a helpful one. I know he would wish to have, not only the acclaim of this House of Commons but the acclaim of all the provincial legislatures in Canada for the work done by Jack Miner. When that day comes, then he could again introduce a bill which would give effect to that desire.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APRIL 10 AS JACK MINER NATIONAL WILD LIFE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not like to see the hon. member's bill killed by the minister in this way. I would suggest to the minister that duringthe recess this bill should go either to the committee on natural resources, mines and all that or be considered by the select committee considering Indian affairs, or taken up in the recess with the provinces and municipalities.
There is a principle to consider in connection with this bill. Our countryside is perhaps one of the most beautiful in the world, and yet I have heard many tourists complain of its reckless destruction, and anything which the government can do to prevent this destruction will help to preserve a natural asset for years to come. Our roads are also another great asset, although it is true that more people have been killed on the great roads, at level crossings and elsewhere, than were killed in the great war. Roads help to open up a country. The great lake Muskoka district is a beautiful one; yet it, like others, is being wiped out by the wilful destruction of the countryside. Nothing has contributed more to the education of the people than the motor car.
There is some merit to this bill which is sponsored by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who always adds a great deal of light to any discussion in which he takes part.
The Hamilton-Dundas highway runs through one of the most beautiful market-garden districts in Ontario; yet I never saw such destruction of the countryside, the wild flowers, the birds, in my life, and many visiting people have expressed the same view. I hope that the minister will consider these suggestions and that during the recess some of the officials will take up this question with the provinces and municipalities and get some action.
We remember Cowper in "The Task" when he speaks of the beauty of the old English countryside and says:
I *would not enter on my list of friends
(Though graced with polish'd manners and fine sense.
Yet wanting sensibility), the man
Who needlessly sets foot upon a worm.
And again he attacks the pleasures of the chase:
Detested sport that feeds on another's pain.
He describes the need of care of the countryside and the bird life of England.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APRIL 10 AS JACK MINER NATIONAL WILD LIFE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for his remarks and for his suggestion that I withdraw the bill now and allow the government to confer with the provinces in connection with the matter he mentioned, namely, the educational matter, and then I can reintroduce a similar bill next year. I do not know
National Wild Life Day

why I should refuse to accept his suggestion, but before doing so I should like to express my warm appreciation of the addresses of all hon. members who have spoken in favour of the bill. All of them have been unanimously in favour of it, including the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown), the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Clark), the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross), the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and in particular perhaps, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradetfe), and I know that had the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) been here before the minister spoke, he, too, would have supported the bill. I quite realize that after the minister has spoken the government supporters have to take back what they said and support the minister. I do not blame them for that because it is likely that I would do so myself if I were over there. In order to have government in this country it is the duty of party followers to be loyal, and I have never objected to that.
I am sure that what has been said in this debate will be helpful to the foundation. I am concerned that Canada recognize the great achievement of the late Jack Miner. The minister has mentioned a number of other distinguished naturalists and all that he has said of them is true. But their achievements were quite different from those of Jack Miner in this regard, that his life was associated with the service he performed through children, and the main purpose of a bill such as this would be to educate the children. I am sure that teachers would welcome an hour or more on a Friday afternoon to teach children the importance of conservation of wild life. The bill was never intended to establish a holiday or anything like that but was patterned after the bills in the United States where many states have wild life day, and there is also a national wild life day. But no other country has had such a character as the late Jack Miner to hang a bill on, so to speak. What other conservationist did work at all comparable with that done by Jack Miner? None that I know of, though all the men mentioned by the minister were great men.
I do not think I need say any more. I shall withdraw the bill and next year reintroduce another bill on the understanding, as the minister indicated, that in the meantime the government will inquire from the provinces if they have any objection. I do not see

why they should have. I am sure they would welcome his inquiries. I cannot conceive of any province not desiring to teach children to conserve wild life. Think of all the insectivorous birds and what a wonderful job they do for Canada and any other country, but how many children know their names or indeed anything about them? Not many. I remember, as a boy going to school, reading a poem by the late Lord Tennyson, the first verse of which ran something like this:
I come from haunts of coot and hern,
I make a sudden sally,
And sparkle out among the fern,
To bicker down a valley.
I remember that as a child one of the first things I wanted to know was, what was a hem? There are two spellings for it, "hern" and "heron"; the poet uses "hern", which may be poetic licence. I wanted to know what a heron was and what a coot was. This kind of thing is educational. I cannot conceive of any educational body not being intensely interested in the opportunity to allow children to be instructed in wild life conservation, to know something about waterfowl, to understand the habits of geese and ducks. It is an interesting study and should be welcomed by boards of education. In the United States the national wild life association of Washington sends out large quantities of literature which are very popular with boards of education throughout the country.
As I said the other day, the Jack Miner foundation is one in which this country will have a part after the present members of the family pass on, because new managers are to be named by the Prime Minister of Canada, the President of the United States, and the treasurer of the foundation. So that we are part of it. The foundation had planned, if the bill had passed, to follow the plan of the national wild life association in the United States. That is all to the good. It would be better here if our national wild life association were not a government association. I do not believe that a government could do as well as the wild life association does in the United States or as the foundation could do here, because of the intense interest of those associated with it to make it a great success and to inculcate the principles of conservation in the minds of youth. I have had letters from various bodies, including sportsmen's and tourists' associations wanting to cooperate. That is all to the good.
However, there is not much use in my prolonging the matter any further at the moment.
I accept the minister's undertaking to consult

speechtext:
Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Peel) moved the second reading of bill No. 3, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have the consent and the direction of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) to proceed with the motion for the second reading of bill No. 3, and I desire at this time to make some observations relative to the legislation proposed. I do so with some pleasure because it is a matter to which both the hon. member for York West and myself have during the past year given close study and careful attention. His constituency and mine adjoin, and in so far as the train whistling problem is concerned which is involved in this amendment to the Railway Act, both of us find our constituents in the same unfortunate and embarrassing dilemma. I should like in the unavoidable absence of the hon. member for York West to pay tribute to the industrious way in which he has pursued the matter in the interests of his constituents, and which has reflected upon my constituents in a very favourable way as well.
The question involved is an amendment to the Railway Act. The notes on the bill itself are, of course, partly explanatory of the purposes and intent and purport of the bill. Roughly speaking, larger places-cities, for instance, and towns-have the right, where railways pass through their midst, to pass a by-law prohibiting the blowing of train whistles within the boundary limits of those municipalities. So far so good. The difficulty which now is arising in many suburban parts is that these suburbs have grown up and their population has increased so that, while they may still only qualify as townships and villages, the frequency of train whistling, with the ever-increasing population, has presented an embarrassing nuisance problem to the residents. I know best, perhaps, the problem of the Lake Shore area between Toronto and Hamilton, because part of that area is in the constituency of Peel which I have the honour to represent. Take, for instance, the township
of Etobicoke, very close to the city of Toronto; the township of York, the village of Long Branch, the township of Toronto and the village of Port Credit, and so on. All along that line of railway are found to-day heavily populated areas, and still some of those municipalities have not the right under the Railway Act to regulate the whistling nuisance which is caused by the tremendous number of trains going to and fro each day.
I take the liberty of detaining the house for a moment to indicate the extent of the problem and how serious it is to the residents. A man named George S. Warner, of the township of Etobicoke, in the constituency represented by the hon. member for York West, took the trouble last fall, by staying awake until the early hours of the morning and making a survey, to ascertain the extent of the nuisance. I shall not go over all the details which appear in a report over his signature, but he speaks of one situation near his own home. He says:
There are six level crossings in my area in less than one mile in a closely congested area of approximately 9,000 people. From 7 in the evening until 7 in the morning thirty trains blow four shrieking blasts for each crossing.
Or, as he refers to it, a "terrible total of 700 sleep-disturbing whistles every night." In connection with that, the medical officer of health for that township and the principal of the large collegiate there, as well as many others who are interested in the matter, have asked the hon. member for York West to bring this matter to the attention of the house. One of the newspapers in my own riding, the Port Credit Weekly, conducted a campaign last fall against the whistling nuisance in the Port Credit area. I have here on my desk only a few of the many hundreds of ballots or coupons which were sent to me, indicating that no small amount of interest has been taken in this problem in that area.
The hon. member for York West and I went to the board of transport commissioners for some relief from our problem. Last fall I received from the board a long report indicating that many people in my constituency had been interviewed and the problem had been gone into very fully, but there seemed to be what on the farm we used to speak of as a nigger in the woodpile, and in this legislation we are trying to get the nigger out of the woodpile; that is the purpose of the amendment. I think the need of this amendment will become apparent when I read a paragraph of the report of the board of transport commissioners. This is what the secretary of that board said in a letter to me:
Railway Act

Mr. W. K. Rogers, assistant superintendent, Canadian National Railways, stated that train movements per twenty-four hours were as high as 134. On a basis of four blasts for each crossing, of which there are two in the village of Port Credit, this would total 1,072 per day or 53 per hour.
He goes on to say that on two particular days the train movements totalled 91 and 96, but these were admittedly light days. Then this is the point I wish to bring particularly [DOT] to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). The report from the secretary of the board goes on:
It must appear fairly obvious from the above, that the complaints on file are well founded. It was pointed out to them that theirs was a problem that would be difficult to solve, inasmuch as the railways were but carrying out the requirements of the law, which law makes no provision for a township or a village taking advantage of section- 308 of the Railway Act.
So that both the hon. member for York West and myself, in following this avenue of approach in an attempt to solve this problem, found ourselves up against a stone wall in the act as it stands at present, particularly section 308. At this point, if I may,
I should like to indicate to the minister just what section 308 of the Railway Act actually says. This is the section, without any proposed amendment:
When any train is approaching a highway crossing at rail level the engine whistle shall be sounded at least eighty rods before reaching such crossing, and the hell shall be rung continuously from the time of the sounding of the whistle -until the engine has crossed such highway.
2. Where -a municipal by-law-
This is the further point involved.
-of a city or town prohibits such sounding of the whistle or such ringing of the bell in respect of any such crossing or crossings within the limits of such city or town, such by-law shall, if approved by an order of the board, to the extent of such prohibition relieve -the company and its employees from the duty imposed by this section.
Therefore the purport and intent of the amendment moved by the hon. member for York West is to enlarge the jurisdiction and power of municipalities which do not qualify as either cities or towns but are known as villages or townships, with large populations in suburban areas, or close by or contiguous to large centres of population, giving them the same privilege and power given to a town or city to pass a by-law in the hope that upon submission to the board of transport commissioners it may receive approval and result in having the train whistling abated.
I do not wish to go on too long with this matter, because it seems to me this is a very simple, yet a very important and urgent

sort of amendment. But I should like to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that what is suggested in this legislation must, I think, be regarded as a move toward the abatement of this nuisance within the limits of public safety. And public safety is paramount. I think that must be said, because, after all, the railways to-day, no matter how much they may cooperate in an attempt to abate the nuisance on their own, by virtue of this section of the Railway Act still find that if they do not blow the whistle or ring the bell they may be in a serious position in case of accident.
I should like to deal with one further point before I sit down. Of course I believe this bill goes a long way toward solving an important problem; but in these congested areas I think the time is coming and in many instances has already arrived when the whole question of grade separation must be dealt with intelligently and effectively. I know that in some of the very instances cited the ultimate solution of the problem may well be grade seiparation. So that I would suggest to the minister that when this bill is given second reading and sent to the aprop-riate committee, some consideration might be given to some changes in the phraseology of the bill itself so that it will not be restricted in its scope only to municipalities which immediately adjoin large cities or populated areas which at present have power to pass by-laws of the kind to which I have just referred. I am anxious that this important point be considered by the committee.
I hope I may have an opportunity to appear before that committee, even though I m-ay not be a member of it, because I should like to see the township of Toronto and the village of Port Credit, in which I am particularly interested,, given an opportunity of coming within any amended legislation. Therefore I hope that will be made clear in the bill when it finally emerges from the committee stage.
I ask for the support and sympathy of the house in connection with this power which, it seems to me, should be given to municipalities which find themselves in such an embarrassing and awkward position as I have just outlined. I also commend this amendment to the Minister of Transport, whose courtesy is so well known in matters of this kind and who, as time goes on, I am quite sure will feel as I do with respect to the merits of the bill.

subtopic: POWER TO PROHIBIT SOUND SIGNALS AT CROSSINGS IN OR NEAR CITIES AND TOWNS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not only in the townships that this nuisance of whistles and bells has been created; it applies equally in the cities and towns. As far as I can see, the only solution of this problem is the electrification of all railways in the Toronto district within a radius of thirty miles of the city. Surely that could be done, w-ith the large amounts the two railway companies are receiving to-day. After all, the Canadian National made most of its money in the province of Ontario, and I think the time has come when the steam railways should do something about the electrification of their systems in the vicinity of Toronto, as they have done in the Montreal area.
The Railway Act provides for equality of treatment. I support the principle of the bill because I know something about it. Under section 275 of the Railway Act the board of transport commissioners is required of its own volition to go out and see these things. As the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said about another department, they should not be just a commission sitting in swivel chairs. They are supposed to go out into the highways and byways and see what is going on and carry on an inspection.
There have been a large number of complaints along the lake-shore road and the Dundas highway and in other parts of the constituency of York West. I remember the time when the city of Toronto bought up all the light, power and electric railway franchises in the two counties of York and Ontario in order to transport the people by cheap fares.
Another section of the Railway Act which has to do with commutation tickets has been violated. Oakville and Brampton have them. That section has not been carried out. In my opinion the board of railway commissioners are empowered to act. They hear applications with regard to these whistle matters, and they do not do anything about it. The board of railway commissioners does not function in the way it should and in the way it did when the late Mr. Justice Mabee was appointed chairman of the commission. As I see it, something has to be done about the electrification of railways in the Toronto district.
Take the Don valley in the constituency which I represent and also in that of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman). When I first bought a house in North Rosedale and lived there for eighteen years the ringing of bells, the sounding of whistles and the shunting all day and night were something that one could hardly imagine. I never heard anything like it in my life. It went on all night long. Complaints were made to the railway commission and applications were made by the township and city, but nothing was done about the matter. The only solution of this problem that I see is for the board of railway commissioners to act on its own volition. It has the power under the Railway Act. Why do they have to wait for an application to be made by a private citizen or a municipality? They have certain functions to perform. In New York state they are compelled to act. If our board of railway commissioners fulfilled their functions we would not have matters like this coming before the house. The Canadian National Railways should do something about the Toronto district. They have plenty of money to build a tunnel in Montreal costing S25 million. Surely they could afford to electrify their system and use the new diesel type of engines they have. There is no reason why something should not be done. I urge that this bill be passed because there is a great deal of force in it.
I call the attention of the house to the last three lines in the bill. I remember an accident a few years ago which happened on the Brown's line, I think it was, near the home of Monsignor O'Leary on Brown's line below Dundas street. In that accident three or four schoolteachers were crossing a railway crossing in a car. There was a good view for half a mile, nothing but farm lands around. The whistle was blowing, but they did not see the train and three or four people lost their lives. The house will note that the last three lines of this bill relieve the company from any liability or penalty under the section in case of an accident. Therefore an individual will have no action for damages if a person is killed on a level crossing in this district. If that should happen the railway company can plead not guilty by statute. If a person were injured he would have no action for damages in a civil court. Let us not, when we are considering this bill, forget the huge loss of life that takes place at these level crossings in Canada.
