The only changes I can see in this railway bill is that it gives the townships and villages the same rights as a city or town to pass a by-law

Canadian Citizenship

with respect to whistling and ringing of railway bells in their communities. In the town in which I live two main lines, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, run through it. On these two main lines seventy trains travel up and down every day, and there are five level crossings in the town. There are no automatic signals on at any of these crossings. We are in this position. If we appeal to the board of railways commissioners to have the whistling stopped and it is granted and there is a fatal accident the town council is blamed for passing such a by-law. In the town of Port Hope there is a hospital a short distance from these two tracks and the Trinity college school, which is a boarding school. Both institutions are greatly disturbed. I have had several letters from residents of this town asking that something be done to have the blowing of the whistles stopped in the town. If the town passes a by-law to stop the whistling and someone is killed the council is blamed. If we do not do this, then we have to put up with the whistling nuisance. Therefore we are between the devil and the deep blue sea.
In the last few years we have had nine deaths at these crossings. Although I am in favour of having the nuisance done away with by applying to the board of transport commissioners, yet I feel the government should take steps to instal automatic signals on every level crossing in the country. I understand that this can be done by applying to the board. But the municipality must stand the greater part of the cost of installing these signals. As the house knows, the only income available to the municipalities is the tax they levy on small properties and the dog tax, yet they are asked to bear the greater cost of installing these signals. The nuisance is so great that one man said to me, with seventy trains passing through this town every night, whistling and blowing four times each, by the time he jumped out of bed seventy times and back in again, it got on his nerves to such an extent that he did not get any sleep. If the installation of a signal will save a human life, surely it should be done. I ask the government to consider bearing a greater share of the cost of installing these automatic signals, and that they be installed on every level crossing in the country.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
In moving second reading of this bill may I state at the outset I believe this measure parallels the development of Canada as a
TMr. Stephenson.]
nation. The bill arises from the fact of pride, common pride, in the achievements of our country, based upon the great exploits of our people. I would suggest that it symbolizes our aspirations as a nation for the future. When I spoke to the house on first reading last October I concluded with these words- and I beg the indulgence of the house to repeat them to-night:
For the national unity of Canada and for the future and greatness of this country it is felt to be of the utmost importance that all of us, new Canadians or old, have a consciousness of a common purpose and common interests as Canadians; that all of us be able to say with pride and say with meaning:	"I iam a Canadian
citizen."
That, sir, in a general way, sets out the main objective of the bill. But the bill seeks to do more than that. As I shall endeavour to show, it seeks to avoid many complexities and confusions which arise from existing legislation. For some time now, indeed for many years, it has been felt in the country and in the house that the time has arrived when ambiguities arising out of the Naturalization Act- both the act before 1914, and the one of 1914-the Canadian Nationals Act, and the Immigration Act, should be treated in such a way as to provide an unambiguous definition of the status of Canadian citizenship.
It may be of interest to note that in 1931 the then Secretary of State, the Hon. C. H. Cahan, felt exactly as I do with regard to the necessity of removing the anomalies in existing legislation. He felt, as I feel, that the time had come when Canada, having matured into full nationhood, should give her people the right of being able to designate themselves Canadian citizens. In these words he expressed his views:
I think we have reached the stage in the policy of our national life that we should seriously consider the foundations for its future development. For sixty-four years we have had a very satisfactory material development. We have been promoting great national works, grafting out new provinces, providing organized governments for the great Northwest Territories and I think we have succeeded far beyond the expectations of the fathers of confederation in the material and commercial development of Canada. In connection with that development, however, if we are to assume the status of a nation within the British commonwealth, we must also assume very serious duties and responsibilities. Among the responsibilities resting upon the (parliament of Canada is that of framing a clear definition of "Canadian nationals" for whom the government and parliament are responsible, whether they are resident in the dominion or temporarily resident outside of our territorial jurisdiction. So long as they retain the status of Canadian national, they should, in my opinion, be treated as such and as holding a Btatus within the dominion equal to that which any others individually enjoy.

C anadian Citizenship
That was the view of a diligent secretary of state, who sought to put before the parliament of that day, not in the details of the present bill, but following its main principle, the measure to which I am now asking the house to give second reading. That bill was proceeded with to the stage of second reading, but for some reason or another not made fully known at the time, the then secretary of state advised the house that he was not proceeding with the bill. But that his convictions had not been disturbed, in spite of the decision not to proceed, is noted in the observations he made later in this house in 1937, when he used these words:
I repeat that sometimes I fear we have more of the colonial spirit of inferiority than even our fathers and grandfathers had and certainly the time has come in the history of this dominion when, if we seek to ascertain who are Canadians and who are Canadian nationals, we should be able to find it in some substantive enactment outside of the Immigration Act, the real purpose and intent of which is to exclude certain classes of people from obtaining domicile in Canada. Why we should be compelled to look to that act for a definition of who are Canadians, who are Canadian nationals, I cannot understand. I think it is a discreditable condition in which we find ourselves to-day.
So, Mr. Speaker, I say it is a discreditable position in which we find ourselves as a nation among the nations of the world to-day not to be able clearly to address one another with the full sanction of the law and for all purposes as citizens of our own country.
Under this bill we are seeking to establish clearly a basic and definite Canadian citizenship which will be the fundamental status upon which the rights and privileges of Canadians will depend. We hope at the same time to remove a great many anomalies and difficulties which exist under present legislation, as I have noted, and which have not only been irksome and troublesome to the country and its people, but occasioned real hardship to persons who have had the misfortune to be caught in them.
Under the present Canadian Nationals Act, which was passed in 1921, on introduction by the Right Hon. C. J. Doherty, the purpose was to meet certain commitments this country had made as a member of the league of nations, and also to permit our taking advantage of possible nomination to membership in the International Court of Justice. That was the only purpose-the very limited purpose of the Canadian Nationals Act-so that we could say, for the purposes of that act, having in mind its immediate objective, that there was such a thing as a Canadian national.
But the definition of Canadian citizenship in that act was a definition by reference. The only unrelated and existing definition of Canadian citizenship is to be found in the Immigration Act. The Canadian Nationals Act defines a Canadian citizen as one who comes within the meaning of the definition of the Immigration Act.
There are few countries in the world who define their citizenship within the clauses of an immigration act. Even the definition within the Immigration Act is a limited one. It is a definition of citizenship only for the purposes of that act, namely for the purposes of immigration.
The Naturalization Act, passed in this house in 1914, which sought to provide for the application of extra-territorial powers to give to naturalized British subjects in Canada the right to have that designation not only in Canada but throughout the world, followed earlier acts which came into being shortly after 1867. But because of the difficulties, the great injustices, the natural pride and urge of every Canadian, the time has come, and I think unmistakenly, if I can judge by reactions of public opinion throughout this country since the introduction of the bill, when not only those on whose shoulders rested the primary responsibility of representing Canada on the fields of battle during the late war, but all Canadians generally, proud of their country, have reached the stage where, in the form of a legal enactment, they want an undoubted right to be able to call themselves Canadian citizens, the right to be able to say when they cross the border that they are citizens of Canada, the right to be given a passport on which the words "Canadian citizen" will appear. They want the right, in other words, which is recognized by every country, and every government in every country with respect to its own people.
I would point out that under the present legislation, the three acts I have mentioned, the wife of a Canadian citizen, or a person born out of Canada whose father was a Canadian national at the time of his birth, would be entitled to receive a Canadian passport, even if it was perfectly clear that the applicant did not possess Canadian citizenship under the Immigration Act. There is also the problem of the prohibited immigrant to Canada.
The curious picture is thus presented of a person who cannot enter Canada under the Immigration Act being entitled to receive a Canadian passport which requests assistance and protection for him in foreign countries. This is but one of many like instances that could be recited of the confusion which now exists and which by this bill we have made an honest and complete attempt to remedy.
Canadian Citizenship

Generally speaking, by this bill we are seeking to make the status of Canadian citizenship the paramount national status of *persons who are Canadians. I find in the administration of my department considerable difficulty in connection with administering certain acts such as the Copyright Act and the Patent Act, largely because of the indefiniteness and, in many instances, the absolute lack of a legal basis for determining nationality, or citizenship as I prefer to call it.
Further, in other departments of government there is great difficulty of administration in connection with matters arising out of the treaty of Versailles and out of the early reparations treaty. I suspect that if this bill is not made law we shall have difficulty in dealing with some subsequent reparations agreement that will arise as a result of the war from which we have just emerged.
Considering the question of convenience and the recognition of our status as a growing nation, I submit that I need not labour the great need, urgency and desirability of having this measure passed. As I said, other departments of government are interested in the matter. For instance, the Department of External Affairs has a vital interest in the determination of status because it is concerned with the issuing of passports and with the diplomatic protection of Canadians and Canadian interests abroad. I am told that this is made exceedingly difficult by reason of the lack of any national status test. Neither the Canadian Nationals Act nor the Naturalization Act nor the Immigration Act afford any satisfactory way out as far as this matter is concerned.
Then, again, that department is concerned with the maintenance of understandings which exist with other members of the British commonwealth concerning nationality questions and with general international problems and arrangements concerning the protection of Canadians and Canadian interests in enemy and enemy occupied countries. The present legislation does not furnish any adequate test of personal status for this purpose. That department is also concerned with the definition and position of Canadians and Canadian interests in treaty negotiations; with the problems of deportation, both coming and going; with the problems that arise out of naturalization and the requirements of the revocation of naturalization certificates; with the need of establishment by proper legislation of a status which would determine the right of a person to regard himself as a Cana-

dian and of documentary evidence which would enable an individual to claim such a position.
This measure in its present form will meet the difficulties I have enumerated in the case of the Department of External Affairs, as well as meet some of the problems that I have mentioned in the administration of the Department of the Secretary of State. When the bill is passed it will mean that a Canadian citizen will be entitled as a Canadian citizen to receive a Canadian passport, to enter Canada, to be deported to Canada under circumstances in which deportation is required under existing principles of international law, to receive diplomatic protection, to enjoy full political and economic rights within- Canada and to own a Canadian ship or part of a ship.
Hon. members may find it rather unusual that these six enumerated benefits, among others, will follow from the passage of this bill. The fact is that there are constant administrative difficulties with regard to these six minimum requirements of nationality in the department of immigration, the Department of External Affairs and the Department of the Secretary of State.	[DOT]
The measure before the house is not without its complications. I may say frankly that the bill in its present form represents a great deal of effort and study on the part of the officials of four departments of government, the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Justice, the Department of Immigration and the Department of the Secretary of State.
My colleague, the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), authorizes me to say that when this measure becomes law it will be followed by an amendment to the Immigration Act which will remove from section 2 of that act the only real definition, although for a limited purpose, of Canadian citizenship that is to be found. As I said at the outset, it will be remembered that the definition of a Canadian national in the Canadian Nationals Act is a definition by reference.
This measure is one that has behind it no political purpose. I think it is one that will commend itself to the consideration of all hon. members. When we come to the committee stage I shall welcome any suggestions which may be made to improve the draftsmanship, if that be found possible, or even the content of the bill in order to make the measure as nearly efficient as it is humanly possible to make it.
One thing we hope-to do, following the passage of this measure, is to provide a more effective and impressive ceremony of admis-

Canadian Citizenship
sion into the Canadian family. Our citizenship is made up not only of people bom in this country and of people who acquired domicile as British subjects under the Immigration Act, but of many thousands of new Canadians living in all parts of our country who have come from other lands and who have made a notable contribution to the development of Canada. There are people who came from many parts of central Europe and who are now living and working as Canadians on our farms and in our factories. Many of those people came here without being able to speak the two languages of the country and without being accustomed to its traditions. Most of them have rendered notable service to Canada. We should not lose the opportunity of impressing ourselves and reminding them that just as we are glad to welcome them to our shores, now that they are here they should enjoy with us the full measure of partnership in the Canadian community.
There will be others who will come after this bill has passed and who in the years ahead will add to our numbers and share our traditions and aspirations. Many hon. members have expressed themselves on this subject, notably the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). We are convinced of the desirability of emulating the form of ceremony which characterizes the admission of persons into United States citizenship. An attempt is made to impress upon potential United States citizens the nature of the undertaking as well as to indicate the opportunities and the privileges and the responsibilities of a United States citizen.
It may be that in Canada for some reason or another ceremonies of admission here and there in the country have been a little more perfunctory than we would have liked to have them, and it is our determination under the statutory provisions of this bill to frame regulations that will make these ceremonies more than an ordinary procedure, and one of a memorable character.
Many hon. members belong to service clubs, and the ritual of attendance and admission into these clubs oftentimes is so impressive as to place in the candidate's mind an indelible iippression of the nature of the obligation assumed. But there is no finer club in the world so far as we are concerned than the club that I would characterize as the Canadian family. We should want, therefore, to impress upon new Canadians whom we shall welcome and want to share in our national endeavours that they are joining no mean society but a society that will give them
freedom and an opportunity perhaps that they have not. had in other lands, and at the same time to point out to them the nature of the obligation undertaken and tell them something of the kind of country and the kind of general political basis of the Canadian society itself.
I have endeavoured since becoming Secretary of State to perfect the machinery of these ceremonies to the extent that time and the law allow-ed. I have gone myself to a number of these ceremonies. I went a few months ago to the city of Toronto, where perhaps these ceremonies are performed in as fitting a manner as one will find in any part of the country. There His Honour Judge Parker, the senior county court judge, who for a number of years has taken a great interest in these matters, has had ceremonies which I know have made a- deep impression upon every new Canadian who has obtained Canadian naturalization in that city and through the avenue of that particular judge. I have gone to these ceremonies and to others, not because my personal presence is of any account but because as minister of the crown, speaking in the name of the government and the people of Canada, I have found it useful to invite and to welcome these new Canadians to our national family. I believe that if we pursue this approach to the matter -we shall do a great deal to make these new Canadians more valuable citizens who will the more readily appreciate the great opportunity which under our law we hope we shall be able to give them.
I wish to pay a tribute to-night to such organizations as the Daughters of the Empire, to Canadian and service clubs, to Mr. Justice Dysart of Winnipeg, to His Honour Judge Gordon of Windsor, men and .organizations who have in a very special manner contributed greatly to the kind of work which I think will be found to be a very valuable ancillary feature to the bill now before the house.
In the new Citizenship 'branch, which has been transferred to the Secretary of State from the Minister of National War Services, an opportunity is given of dealing effectively and more fully not only with foreign language newspapers but with new Canadian groups. We hope to be able to use, as I shall show when we come to a detailed discussion of the bill, this new Citizenship branch as a means of furthering the kind of suggestions which were made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and others when speaking in this house two or three years ago.
The bill is not in its essence a difficult one. even though some of the clauses may require more than ordinary attention. It will be of
Canadian Citizenship

assistance to non. members to note that out of the 47 sections of the bill 18 are virtually reenactments of existing sections and 17 are new. What we are dealing with is really a comprehensive revision of the Naturalization Act done in such & way as to produce a status of Canadian citizenship that will be sufficiently inclusive to serve as a basic definition for immigration and for all general purposes and that will eliminate the need for subordinate definitions.
Hon. members will have observed from an examination of the bill that it is divided into seven parts, in addition to three preliminary sections and two concluding schedules. The three preliminary sections form what is really an interpretative portion containing the definitions necessary for the proper drafting of the substantive parts.
It has been a long-standing source of irritation to many Canadians to be told on occasion, in reply to a question as to their national status, that there is no such thing as a Canadian and that some other national status has to be declared. In this bill we now provide that so far as any questions coming within the competence of the Canadian government are concerned the answer "Canadian citizen" in reply to an inquiry as to national status shall be sufficient. So far as national status is concerned the description "Canadian citizen" will hereafter be sufficient.
Part I of the bill deals with natural-bom Canadian citizens. The first section of this part attempts to set forth that persons now in being are immediately to have the status of Canadian citizens as of right of birth. The people who will be natural-born Canadian citizens are of two classes, those who are born in Canada or on a Canadian ship, and those who were born to Canadian parents outside Canada before the passing of the act, except of .course for such of these persons as may have become aliens before the act comes into effect. There are refinements in the bill, but on a broad generalization those are the categories of people now in being who will be natural-born Canadian citizens immediately.
The second thing done in part I is to define what persons born after the act comes into force shall be natural-born Canadian citizens. In general, the provisions here for persons born before the act are similar to those to which I have referred and do not differ greatly from the definitions of a natural-born British subject that are now contained in the Naturalization Act. The principal difference is this, that in future all Canadian children bom abroad will have to be registered within two years either at a diplomatic, consular or trade commissioner's office or in Ottawa. Hitherto
TMr. Martin.]
registrations have not been necessary in all cases of children born abroad who have acquired the status provided for in existing legislation. There is, I believe, good reason for this. There is a slightly greater strictness in the new bill. Hereafter Canadian children bom abroad will as Canadian citizens have the right of entry into Canada. They have never had this before. In giving this important right it is felt necessary to have some record and some form of evidence that will serve for immigration purposes. Children born in Canada 'will in all cases have birth certificates. In a parallel manner we are requiring the registration of children born abroad, in order that there may be a basic record to establish their rights as Canadian citizens.
Apart from registration there is nothing that is essentially new or different in part 1. The relevant provisions concerning foundlings and children born after the death of their father fill in gaps that exist in existing legislation.
Part II of the bill deals with the second broad division of Canadian citizens, those who were not bom to citizenship but acquire it at a later stage. There are two cases to provide for: the people who are to be Canadian citizens at once because of action taken before the passage of this act; and those who may become Canadian citizens hereafter. Provision is made to cover persons other than natural-born Canadian citizens who are to be Canadian citizens immediately upon the coming into force of the act. This section I will frankly state has been a particularly difficult one to draft. It was revised repeatedly in successive drafts of the bill. The present section is somewhat altered from the form in which it was presented in the bill introduced in this house last October by way of first reading. I think the section now says what we wanted it to say. The broad intention is to provide that the people who have been naturalized in Canada hitherto, non-Canadian British subjects who have resided in Canada for five years or more, and non-Canadian women who married Canadians and have come to live in Canada, shall become Canadian citizens immediately. This matter has been thought over and discussed carefully, and I think the definitions will cover all those who should be Canadian citizens at once, and no others.
The second portion of part II provides for future acquisition of Canadian citizenship through naturalization. The qualifications for future naturalization are almost exactly the same as those now in force, except that only

Canadian Citizenship,
one year of residence, rather than five, will be required of persons who served out of Canada in our armed forces during time of war. Actually, because the time that a man has served in the armed forces of Canada is to be taken as a period of residence in Canada, this will mean that men in the armed forces will in fact not have to spend any prior time in Canada before being admitted into Canadian citizenship, on the theory that if a man is prepared to fight for this country there should be no hesitation in granting him what we can grant by way of labelling him a citizen of this country.
Although it is not set forth in the Naturalization Act, but only in the regulations, we have since 1943, required "a declaration of intention" to become naturalized to be made before actual naturalization is applied for. This declaration has to be made at least one year and not more than five years before naturalization takes place. As the house will recall, essentially the same requirement is made in the United States. In future, under the bill now before the house, such declaration will be necessary for aliens who wish to become naturalized in Canada, but not for the wives or husbands of Canadians or from nonCanadian British subjects. With regard to the other naturalization requirements, a certain relaxation is provided in that twenty years' residence may substitute for a knowledge of French or English.
I will frankly say to the house at this stage why that provision was put in there. It came to my attention not very long ago that a man who had lived in this country, in the province of Saskatchewan, for thirty-two years had for reasons best known to himself not been able to acquire the slightest kind of proficiency in either of the two official languages of this country, and under the act the judge was precluded from granting him the right to receive a certificate of naturalization. It later developed that this particular person had sent two sons to fight in the armed forces of Canada; one of these sons had won the Distinguished Flying Cross and the other gave his life for Canada. I felt, and I hope the house will agree with me, that that kind of person is entitled to Canadian citizenship. This provision will enable the naturalization of many people, especially in western Canada, who have proved to be good citizen material but who have not for one reason or another learned to speak French or English.
On the other hand, there is a slightly greater strictness in the new qualifications in the bill in requiring a knowledge "of the responsibilities
and privileges of Canadian citizenship." Coming into the Canadian family is, of course, a great honour, but it entails certain obligations; and we hope in an objective manner, without trying to coerce, merely to lay before these new Canadian citizens the recognized facts of the Canadian scene, to lay before them through properly prepared material, prepared perhaps by non-governmental organizations who have the sanction of educational authorities, historians and so on, facts which will inform them not only of the opportunities and the privileges which they will acquire as future Canadian citizens, but of the obligations, for we cannot emphasize too much that along with privileges go obligations in citizenship. As one reads the report of the judges who sit on these applications for naturalization, one of the salutary things to note is that in so many instances, in fact the vast majority, there seems to be a recognition of the duties which these new citizens have to acquire. I attended recently a ceremony in Toronto when thirty-two persons were admitted into Canadian "citizenship" under the existing legislation, and I use the word "citizenship" here in quotation marks because it is not a correct statement of the legal situation. One of these new citizens wrote to me afterwards stating that he wanted to do something to show his appreciation of the kind of country to which he had been admitted. Both his mother and his father, though civilians, had been slaughtered by the nazis. He had come to this country in 1933, had returned in 1935 for two years, and came back at the end of that time. He was so impressed with the opportunities of this country that he wanted to tell the government and the people of his appreciation; and what could he do? I told him that it would be very difficult for me to suggest, other than that I trusted he would live up to the obligations entailed in being a good citizen of this country. I am pleased to state that that man showed his appreciation of the work of Judge Parker and the attempts that were being made by the naturalization branch, by giving to one of our universities, only Saturday last, the sum of $35,000 to be used by a particular university in encouraging and disseminating desirable information about Canadian life and the great opportunities which this country affords.
With regard to the other naturalization requirements, as I say, the relaxation consists in giving a knowledge of these responsibilities as well as these privileges. Apart from these minor points the general naturalization requirements remain unchanged.
Canadian Citizenship

have suffered, to the detriment of this magnificent country, it is from a feeling of divisiveness-lack of that fervent and urgent unity that can make a people work together as a great community with conviction that the welfare of all is the goal of their effort. It is not enough to be a good "Bluenose" or a good Ontarian or a good Albertan. Sectional differences and sectional interests must be overcome if we are to do our best for Canada. The only way this can be done is through encouraging a feeling of legitimate Canadianism. No matter where we come from or what our origins, French, English, Scandinavian, Scottish, Ukrainian, Irish or whatever else, one thing at least we can all be, and that is Canadians.
Citizenship means more than the right to vote; more than the right to hold and transfer property; more than the right to move freely under the protection of the state: citizenship is the right to full partnership in the fortunes and in the future of this nation.
With this bill we are linking our past with our future. We are saying to history and to our posterity: Here is the definition of Canadianism. Here is the common status in Canada, a common stake in the welfare of the country, a common Canadian citizenship.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
With much, if not all, that has been said by the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) I am in agreement, particularly where he said that this measure symbolizes our aspirations as a nation.

As I conceive it, this measure translates into the days of peace the unity of our nation in war. During two wars men without regard to racial origin served this nation as Canadians. Now the opportunity and the privilege is to be given to them in peace to serve their nation in the years to come as Canadians.
The minister has gone at some considerable length into the questions of domicile, citizenship and naturalization, matters most difficult of concept and interpretation. I realize that this bill goes a long way to resolve many of the difficulties that prevail in these_ subjects; nevertheless I am sure that in the committee stage all of us will be able to contribute some suggestions that may result in beneficial improvements of the bill.
This is one measure where political considerations fade and where we as Canadians can view it free and untrammeled. With the bill the official opposition is in agreement. Indeed in one of the first utterances of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), after he was chosen as the leader of this party, in Kingston at a memorial service to the memory of Sir John A. Macdonald in 1043 he called upon the people of Canada to establish in this country a citizenship free from racial origin and unhyphenated. He called upon the people to carry out the dream of founders and builders of confederation that all may be privileged tocall ourselves Canadians.	,
"This bill achieves a lifelong dream of mine. Ever since my earliest days I have advocated the necessity for a change in the attitude in the law and of officialdom toward Canadians.. One criticism that I voiced on. the first occasion that I ever spoke in this chamber was that the bureau of statistics in insisting on the census being taken by racial origin was denying that citizenship which Canadians had the right to ask for, and which our friends and kinsmen across the line have established for many years.
I realize that there has been a Canadian nationality, in an abstract sort of way, for many years, under the acts referred to by the minister. But that citizenship has been denied, in effect when in each succeeding census paternal racial origin has been required of our citizens.	_
This is an important piece of legislation and will give to Canadians a new vista of their responsibilities and privileges as citizens. But legislation of itself can never build a united citizenship. If there is one thing on this occasion that we should do, when we pass this bill and make it the law of the country, it is to determine that individually, henceforth, we owe ourselves the compulsion, regardless of

Canadian Citizenship
our racial origin, of understanding each other's point of view. We must dedicate our determination to encourage and develop in this country mutual trust and mutual tolerance. Above all, we must restrain the undermining of our Canadian confederation through encouraging or developing a dislike of Canadians of other racial origins, for Canada's destiny and Canada's future can and will never be achieved on the basis of racial prejudice.
The minister has said that Chnada has served civilization well in two wars. But the prophetic dreams of nationhood, the vision of Macdonald and Cartier, remain as yet to be completed^-Legislation of itself will not complete it. [Canada must develop, now that we achieve this citizenship, unity out of diversity -a diversity based on non-homogeneous peoples of many religions, peoples of clashing economic differences based on distances, and jurisdictional differences as between federal and provincial authoritiesjThe great challenge to our generation is to fuse these clashing differences, and to build for that unity which, beginning with the dreams of the fathers of confederation, has been cemented by a common sacrifice in two wars.
I repeat that in my opinion one of the most destructive features that has prevented the creation of an unhyphenated nation has been the census requirements, carrying forth from generation to generation racial origin, and not service and citizenship as a basis of registration.
I remember well discussing this matter in the house on August 11, 1944, upon which occasion the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) gave the promise to the people of Canada that at the earliest possible occasion he would bring in a measure to assure an unhyphenated Canadian citizenship. Instead of repeating the arguments I then used, may I with the indulgence of the house repeat the words I then uttered. We were then in the midst of a war.
The minister has mentioned an example of sacrifice and service to our country on the part of one of alien origin. As he uttered those words my thoughts went back to an occasion in 1942 when, while visiting a town in southern Saskatchewan, a man came up to me and asked me whether because his son was serving as an air gunner he was being discriminated against because he, the father, came from Germany a matter of twenty years before. I told him that such was not the fact. Proud he was of the service of that son. Two weeks later the boy received the Distinguished Flying Medal; later on he was commissioned. Throughout Saskatchewan to-day, in the homes of families the parents of which came from continental Europe, are to be found young men who were
honoured in the service with decorations, young men proud of their citizenship and, what is even more important, prepared to fight for that citizenship which had been gained only a few years before.
The words I uttered on that occasion were these:
As one wads the casualty lists each day one is impressed with the fact that without regard to racial origin Canadians are living and dying for their country and their empire. Yet when these young Canadians return ,to this country, what do they come back to? They come back/ to a. Canada which insists that they shall not) designate themselves as Canadians, but shall prefix their paternal national origin, regardless of the number of generations their families have! been in this country.	__j
Then a little later on:
As I have said before, no one thinks of Mr. Roosevelt as a Dutch-American. No one thinks of General Eisenhower as a German-American. No one thinks of Mayor LaGuardia of New York as an Italian-Americam. They are great Americans. We perpetuate this thing every ten years in our census, the excuse being that it is necessary bo have the information as to ethnic groups.
And I concluded with these words:
Those who serve in the Canadian' armed forces are proud of the "Canada" on their shoulder straps, and without regard to hyphenated considerations. While they serve they are Canadians. I ask the Prime Minister 16 round out this great programme which he has placed before the house in the last few days for the benefit and rehabilitation of our men who serve by making the necessary amendments which will once for >ald and without .regard to origin, enable men and women of this country to call themselves Canadians, and by so doing unite this country as never before.
The Prime Minister followed me on that occasion, with these words, which to-day have been translated into the bill now before the house:
I wish to conclude by referring to what my hon. friend said about hoping'that we might, in some way, find it possible to have the citizens of this whole nation1 bound together as Canadians and so recognized and recorded in all government records and 'registrations. He said that, without regard to racial origin, Canadians are living and dying for their country, .and that, above everything else, we should see particularly as respects those brave men who have .been fighting overseas, that upon their return they should be all classed as Canadians, He hoped that, irrespective of racial origin, they would be recognized as Canadians without having to put *any prefixes before their names. May I say to my hon. friend that in that I am in entire and wholehearted agreement with him. I cannot express too strongly the feeling I have that some of these practices which have been carried on by the census branch for statistical purposes, or possibly for ethnological purposes-I believe that is the way it is described-might he done away with. I would be happy to join with my hon. friend and with any others in seeking to

Canadian Citizenship
do my part to see absolute recognition, or recognition made in an absolute way of men and women who were born in this country, and those who have become Canadian citizens being regarded as Canadians first, foremost and all the time,..
I cannot understand the idea behind the census that blood counts should loom so large in determining Canadian citizenship. When the statistics were collected they were inaccurate. As a matter of fact, the manner in which nationality was determined is set forth in the instructions issued for the last census. These are contained in a pamphlet, a page of which I have before me, and are as I follows:
As a general rule a person's racial origin is to j be traced through his father, e.g., if a person's ! father is English and his mother French, the racial origin shall be entered as English, while i a person whose father is French and whose j mother is English, shall be entered as French.
On the basis of that the ethnological argument disappears of itself. In the United States the idea that racial origin is important was done away with many years ago. Under the census regulations of that country the only persons who are required to register on the basis of racial origin are those who are naturalized, the only separation in the registration being that those of the negro, Indian, Chinese and Japanese races are required so to I register.
This bill is an important step forward. In my opinion it will do more to join this dominion together in unity in the days of peace than any other measure that has come before this parliament. But within the last few days something has happened that I think should be brought to the attention of the house because it indicates that even now the rights of Canadian citizens are not being respected as they should be. I referred this afternoon to order in council P.C. 6577, passed on October 23, 1945. The preamble to that order in council reads:
And whereas it is therefore deemed necessary, by reason of the war, for the security, defence, peace, order [DOT]and welfare of Canada that provision as hereinafter set forth be made for the arrest and deportation of persons in Canada suspected of being deserters from the United States forces or of being absent from the United States forces without leave.
This order in council passed in October, 1945, provides that any person suspected may be arrested without warrant. It provides that any person arrested who does not sign a release permitting his deportation to the United States shall be brought before an immigration board and the question determined as to whether or not he is a deserter from the United States army. As far as that order in

council is concerned, if the purpose were to assure a mutual exchange of deserters as between the countries, I would not argue against it, in so far as it affects American citizens. But what I do object to is this: Whereas under the extradition law of this country no Canadian can be deported for an offence committed beyond Canada, except certain designated offences, this order in council is passed and provision is made whereby a native-born Canadian or a Canadian citizen may be deported to another nation at the request of that nation. That is a denial of the rights of Canadian citizenship.
What has happened in the last few days in Winnipeg? A Canadian by the name of MeCloy went to the United States in 1929 and joined the United States army. Later on, he went absent without leave and was sentenced subsequently to two years' imprisonment. He escaped after a period of six months and came back to Canada in September, 1939. He joined the Canadian army and went overseas and served until August, 1945, when he received an honourable discharge.
On March 26, 1946, this man was arrested, put in gaol and later granted bail. When I endeavoured to ask a question about this matter of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) this afternoon he did not give me very much assistance in having it answered. This was a matter of great moment to a Canadian citizen. The minister glossed it over as being unimportant. The man came up to-day before the immigration board in Winnipeg. I am informed that the evidence against him consisted of a letter from Mr. Hoover of the F.B.I. in Washington and another letter from another official in Washington. The man went on the stand in his own defence, and after he gave his evidence the commissioner said that he had received instructions that the matter was to be held in abeyance for the time being.
This order in council was passed after the war by this government when it realized that it could not get through an extradition treaty that it had dangled before this house last session. That order in council denies to Canadians the right to be tried in their own country and not in any other country or at the direction of any other country. Furthermore, it made retroactive on October 23, 1945. an offence that was not extraditable until the order in council in question was passed. Is this another order in council that somehow found its way into the mill without being properly examined?

Canadian Citizenship
I suggest to the minister that the order in council be amended so that it will not cover Canadian citizens and make them deportable for military offences. This is but another example of orders in council passed by the government that would never be passed by this parliament, an order in council denying to Canadian citizens their rights and depriving them of the privileges incident to Canadian citizenship, the privileges which were so eloquently stated by the Secretary of State.
This order in council cannot be glossed over with suave phraseology. I ask the minister, and I know Canadians in all parts of this country would ask the minister also if they had the opportunity, to change it, to alter it and to revoke it so that it will not make Canadian citizens subject to deportation for trial in any other country except under legislation passed by this parliament.
I pass on to another phase. The minister dealt somewhat briefly with section 10. Section 10 provides, among other things, that a British subject coming to Canada from the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Ireland or Newfoundland cannot become a Canadian citizen unless he files notice of intention with the court and unless he comes before the court in the same way as any other person coming from any other country would be required to do. I ask the minister to explain why at this time when we in all parts of the empire are desirous in the interest of our own security to bind still closer the various parts of the empire together, should a British subject coming into Canada and properly entering this country under our immigration law be required to go through the same formalities as persons coming from other parts of the world?
I ask, too, this question: Is it not a dangerous principle to adopt at this time? Is it not one which may well strike at the unity of British citizenship everywhere within this empire?
These are questions which I think the minister should have answered. But he went over that section very quickly and indicated that there was a very small change made. There is a very important change made because for the first time in our history we are requiring a British citizen, under a common king and with a common loyalty, coming to this country to have to go through the same formalities as those coming from foreign countries.
Having established the basis of Canadian citizenship and having given a new unity to this country, I suggest that citizenship, if it is to mean what our citizenship does mean, 63260-33
requires that at this time-I referred to this incidentally the other day-we should consider the adoption by Canada of a Bill of Rights. There have been recent infringements upon citizenship by this government which have been a denial of the heritage that is ours. But Canadian democracy means something when public opinion speaks. The order in council P.C. 6444 of October 5 last has passed into history only because of the force of public opinion in this country, for when the people, realized what its provisions meant to them individually, the government found itself forced to revoke that order in council.
I may be asked, why do we need a Bill of Rights? The British North America Act contains no personal safeguards against unwise or discriminatory legislation that might be passed by federal governments. It vests in the Minister of Justice or in the government the power to annul provincial encroachments on our rights, but it contains nothing to prevent the government of this country by order in council from doing things which deny to Canadians the rights that flow from the achievement of Canadian and British citizenship. Some may ask me why the British North America Act does not contain such a Bill of Rights. I do not know. But I believe this, that when the fathers of confederation drafted that act the theory of personal liberty was so embedded in English common law that the fathers of confederation did not believe that further safeguards cf individual liberty were necessary.
The United States of America had no Bill of Rights in its original constitution, but it found it necessary to establish a Bill of Rights in order to prevent infringements upon its citizenship which, with too great regularity in recent months, in continuation of what was taking place during the war, have characterized this government under order in council.
In the United States, federal and provincial legislatures under their Bill of Rights were forbidden to interfere with certain basic rights common to all citizens, regardless of race, religion or qolour. Freedom of religion, freedom of the press, freedom of assembly, freedom from unreasonable searches and seizures was guaranteed. In the Bill of Rights of the United States it is provided that no person may be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law.
The order in council P.C. 6577, and the order in council of October 5, 1945, P.C. 6444, which I believe will always be remembered as the forgotten order in council, interfere with the fundamental rights of citizenship which were referred to by the Secretary of State.

Canadian Citizenship

Ts it not time that in this country as in Great Britain these rights shall not be interfered with except under a law passed by the parliament of Canada?
When I think of the abrogation of habeas corpus in recent months I find upon an examination of British constitutional development that only nine times in British history was it interfered with in Britain, and then only by statute or under powers contained in a statute to abrogate habeas corpus. We grant the greatest privilege to an individual, that of Canadian citizenship, conveying as it does as well the right of British citizenship. We have gone a step forward. We are making a great advance under this bill. Now let us go one step farther and assure to generations yet to come and assure to our people who will become Canadian citizens that they shall not be denied at any time in the future by order in council those rights that ordinarily are incident to our citizenship.
My time has almost elapsed, but I should like to say this too. In the development of a Canadian nationality everything should be done by the government to encourage and develop Canadian literature and drama and art. The minister has taken a great interest in his department of state. His officials and the officials of other departments worked hard in the drafting of this bill which in every section reveals careful application and much study. I believe that his department might well be utilized as a department for the purpose of widening still further our Canadian citizenship. I believe that his department should establish scholarships available to worthy students to encourage the study of Canadian literature, drama and art, to the end that we should have not only a citizenship but a [DOT] distinctive Canadian art and a distinctive Canadian culture. What would the development of a department like that mean? It would stimulate and support artistic endeavours and assure that Canadian writers, musicians, painters and others would have the support which, only the state can give. It would assure that Canadians would extend their cultural heritage for the benefit of Canadians of this and future generations; for we must not forget that one of the most trying problems in this country to-day is that having given our young Canadians an opportunity of securing a wide education, when they have finished that education, too often by reason of the greater monetary attractions of the United States the cultural development which they should have left in our country is lost to us because there is no department of government to encourage and stimulate their endeavours and to assist them.

For 140 years my ancestors on both sides have made this country their home. For 140 years they and other Canadians have been denied true citizenship. They have been denied the use of those proud words which the minister used: "I am a Canadian.' All my life I have hoped for this day. I believe it means much to this country and to our future. Canada to me means more than the ownership of acres; it means a citizenship which maintains in this part of North America the highest heritage of British peoples everywhere in the world. It means to Canadians, without regard to racial origin, freedom and tolerance and liberty. It is because it means those things to me, sir, that from time to time during the period of the war and since,
I have been critical of the invasions and encroachments on our rights and on these principles of citizenship which constitute the heritage of British peoples.
To-day in this world two ideologies face one another. If ever there was a time when we should assert and practise what our citizenship means, it -is now. The minister has given the lead in that regard in the establishment of schools to the end that citizenship will be taught, and also in the ceremonies which hereafter will be established in order to imbue the minds of those who come to our country with what that citizenship will mean to them. But, believing in freedom, I think we give a poor lead to these people when we endeavour to justify the adoption, in times of peace, of totalitarianism in order to oppose totalitarianism. It is our duty and responsibility as Canadian citizens to maintain those principles and traditions which mean so much to us and to guard against infringement of the great principles of freedom; for, sir, the hallmarks of liberty can be erased as a result of the acts of a zealous person who is misdirected, no less than by one who destroys those principles with evil intent. We will give a great citizenship to Canadians hereafter. We will give them freedom-that we promise-in this country. Let us not deny freedom by executive action on the part of the state, for in doing that we destroy all for which our citizenship stands.
The pages of history tell their story. They tell the story that freedom, like capital, cannot be overdrawn, nor can freedom be preserved while it is being destroyed piecemeal fashion.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us, as the minister so eloquently stated, is to give further expression to the progress which Canadians have miade on the road toward sovereignty. It has

Canadian Citizenship
been a gradual progress and evolution; and in laying this bill before parliament the government, I know, is giving way to the desire of the majority of the Canadian people to establish a distinctly Canadian citizenship.
_ Canadian citizenship is a fact to-day, and it is but proper that we give a legal status to that fact. If this condition is true; if a majority of Canadians are anxious to put upon this Canadian citizenship this stamp of legal approval, and if all these eloquent words which the minister has told us are true, I think he should have put a preamble to this bill which would give the development of our sovereignty and express pride in the progress we have made and that we are now ready to put this legal status of Canadian citizenship on the people.
While I am. in full agreement with this measure, which I believe was actuated by the government upon the principles stated by the minister this evening. I have grave doubts as to the legality of parts of this legislation. I say that in all seriousness and in all friendliness towards the minister.
To make my argument clear, I should like to trace briefly the development and the history of naturalization and sovereignty. Prior to 1914, as the minister stated, we had a Naturalization Act under which aliens were made British subjects within Canada only. The adaption by the parliament of Canada of this legislation prior to 1914 was undoubtedly an act of sovereignty on our part. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said at the imperial conference in 1911:
. The power of naturalization is one of the incident .powers of sovereignty and one of the most important attributes of sovereignty.
However, while this old law was an act of sovereignty, we were at that time by no means as sovereign as we are to-day. The old naturalization law was not of much use to a naturalized citizen when he travelled beyond the boundaries of this country, because then he lost his British citizenship and he was a man with no country at all. When I said that we were then not as sovereign as we are now, I may point out that at that time we had no embassies, no legations' no high commissioners and no consulates to which a Canadian might apply for protection in case he got into difficulty -in some foreign country. It was no doubt owing to this state of affairs that in 1914 the British parliament passed an act concerning British naturalization and the status of aliens. This act deals with the naturalization of aliens, and it was provided in part II of the act that it might be adopted by any legislature of a British
possession or dominion, and, if so, then a certificate of naturalization granted by such a dominion should have the same effect as a certificate granted under this act. This meant that if we adopted the Biritish act any persons who were naturalized would be recognized as British subjects all over the world. Pursuant to this British act we passed our own Naturalization Act in 1914; that is the law which is at present in force, and part II of our act is identical with part II of the British naturalization act. However, this enactment of 1914 was no advancement in sovereignty over the old act. It was not passed in consequence of the powers which we possessed under section 91 of the British North America Act, but by virtue of the British statute already referred to, and the British statute gave it legal effect and force.
I have already said that we adopted verbatim, with only minor necessary changes, part II of the British act. We therefore became entitled to issue certificates of naturalization to aliens as British subjects, who were supposed to be recognized as such all over the world; and I presume that was the case. It seems to me that now under this new legislation we want to have a Canadian citizenship, which I endorse and which is quite proper and natural, and at the same time we also wish to legislate as to British nationality. I maintain that we cannot do so, at least not as the present act is worded. If the present bill becomes law we repeal the present Naturalization Act; that is provided in the last or second last section of the bill. By repealing the present act we would also lose our power to pass any legislation as to who shall be a British subject, because we would also repeal the applicability of the British act.
On the strength of this argument I would say that section 26. which says that a Canadian is a British subject, is beyond the powers of this parliament to legislate. I have no personal objection to this section; I rather like it, but I simply doubt the legality of it. Perhaps it was necessary for some reason unknown, but I submit sincerely that only the British parliament can legislate as to who is a British subject. However, I think I have a way out, and I suggest as an alternative to section 26 the following.

Well, instead of suggesting an amendment, as I tried to do, I shall put it in this way. I mentioned that section 26 in my opinion is beyond the powers of this parliament because we have no right to say who is' a British subject. But we can say this, that a Canadian citizen is a subject of His Majesty as sovereign of Canada, and I think that would be the proper way to put this section. I believe such a section would be quite legal and ought to satisfy all persons, while at the same time it is a true statement of the status of a Canadian citizen. It is still debatable just how far we have progressed on the road to sovereignty, but there is no doubt that we have advanced far enough to say who shall be a Canadian citizen. According to the statute of Westminster the dominion has full power to make laws having extraterritorial operation, and since the passing of that statute we have exerted our power extraterritorially. We can now take our nationals anywhere and they will receive protection. There is also no question but that Canada, especially during the last ten years, has been recognized as a sovereign state. The debate this afternoon and the remarks of the minister this evening bear this out. If for no other reason than that, we should assert our right to create Canadian citizens, and in so doing we can assert and emphasize our British connection in a natural and quite legal manner. I think the suggestion I have made as to section 26 should meet the objections of those who have an extreme desire for sovereignty, as well as of those who hold the British connection dear to their hearts.
For these reasons, of course, the act would have to be amended in a great many other places. For instance, it would seem to me that section 22 is beyond the powers of this parliament, in that it presumes to revoke a certificate granted in another country within the British commonwealth, even though this is done with the concurrence of the government of that country. Likewise section 28 is not only ultra vires but is unnecessary, because other nations of the British Commonwealth are sovereign states, just as we are, and we recognize the status of the nationals of sovereign states by the amity of nations.

I do not wish it to be understood from my arguments that I am against the sentiments contained in these sections. I am all in favour of them, but both sections presume some authority which we do not possess. It is up to the British parliament alone to say who is a British subject. I think the way the act is framed it might entail some serious consequences to a naturalized Canadian if he wants to assert his British nationality.
